#6526. Your Horoscope for the New Moon in Scorpio

This lunation is bringing to the light everything that was done in the dark.

New Moons are a time for rejuvenation and manifestation. If you have a lack in your life, then this is the time the collective will work to fill it, whether through a new experience, person, or item. We must make space for beginnings and foolish behavior during new moons. Mind you, we’re all fools when beginning something new, so don’t be scared to get experimental.

For newbies, a New Moon is when the moon conjuncts the sun to the same degree. New moons are for setting intentions and goals to manifest. Take the theme of each new moon (manifestation period) as inspiration to bring forth the best version of yourself! If you find your horoscope helpful or have any questions, please share your horoscope and tag me on social media @monishaholmes.

The New Moon in Scorpio arrives Monday, November 9, 2026, at 2:02 a.m. ET, at 17 degrees Scorpio. I'm actually such a big fan of this new moon, because we're going to see a lot emerging from it—a lot more clarity. Things that were done in the dark are going to be exposed now. But don't expect everything to come out all at once, because new moons are dark for a reason. Look at the sky: it is not bright, it is a dark moon because the Moon sits between Earth and the Sun, meaning the side facing Earth receives no direct sunlight. In astrological terms, that means our emotions are too close to our sense of purpose, that we are not able to recognize how our feelings and ego are influencing life on Earth. We are going to see things unfolding over the next two weeks.This new moon is making a square to Mars, the planet of conflict and drive. A square is an astrological connection that represents friction—think about the phrase “squaring up.” You might be trying to get to the same goal as someone, but you can't exactly agree on how it's going to be done. We may be wanting something that is loud and bold and perhaps even radical. However, this new moon is testing our patience and basically saying “actually, wait.” We need to investigate. We need to understand what's going on before we can make big, dramatic, theatrical changes. We need to do the work of unearthing. Mars is also making a sextile with Venus retrograde in Libra, the last Venus retrograde that we're going to see like this in a while. When Mars sextiles Venus, what these two planets are doing is making a harmonious agreement: Mars is agreeing to expose if Venus is able to give justice, and Venus is willing to get harmony if Mars is willing to put things under a spotlight. This is going to be a very spicy new moon. If you expected boring, please know that boring is not going to be the theme of this week's moon.

Do not expect a downpour of information. We are not going to get a release of what is hidden immediately. Expect for things to take time to adjust, and then eventually information will start to unravel. If situations unfold fast then be careful, accelerated speed may indicate a potential crash out.

Retrogrades are about returns, reflections, re-evaluation. This isn't a time to make any huge, drastic changes or start something completely new. This is a time to look at what was done, how it is affecting us, so that we can begin to plan moving forward. And it's very important that we follow these steps.

Try to zoom out of yourself as the individual and think about what collective or communal justice would be. Perhaps you as an individual felt betrayed or overlooked or disappointed, but chances are, if it's happening in your neighborhood, then it's happening to somebody else on the block. So don't treat things as if they're occurring in isolation. In fact, wisdom comes from learning that very rarely are things happening to just one person.

Make sure that you are not acting out for the sake of acting out. This moon is calling for a sense of decorum, and considering that Pluto is the modern ruler of Scorpio this new moon’s theme is transformation. Currently, Pluto is direct in Aquarius, which means Pluto is governing change happening to the larger community. No change happens in isolation. We may not need huge masses of people to experience a breakthrough, but we do have to be strategic.

Read your Sun sign to gain insight into the version of yourself that you’re maturing into. Read your Rising sign to reflect on your present state. And read your Moon sign for guidance on how to nurture your inner self (no one is perfect). If you find your horoscope helpful, please share it and tag me on social media @monishaholmes.

This new moon lands in your house of transformation—the part of your chart that covers shared money, debt, intimacy, and the things you keep private. Something in a merged arrangement is ready to be looked at honestly: a balance you've been avoiding, a financial tie that needs clearer terms, or a level of closeness that asks for more trust than you've been giving. With Mars—the planet prompting your drive—in a tense angle to this moon, the urge to confront it all at once will be strong. Investigate first. What surfaces over the next two weeks gives you the full picture, and that's what you actually want to act on.Moon lesson: Look at the shared ledger honestly, but don't settle it in one heated conversation.

Your partnerships are the spotlight now — this new moon falls in your house of one-on-one commitments, directly across from your sign. A relationship, contract, or close collaboration is at a starting point, but it's a quiet one. Venus retrograde is asking for a review before a renewal: what was agreed to before may not fit who either of you is now. If an old conversation about fairness resurfaces, that's not a setback, it's the work. Renegotiate in private, take your time, and let any new terms become clear after the 13th before you lock them in.Moon lesson: A partnership can start fresh—after the old terms get an honest review.

This moon lights up your house of health, daily routines, and work habits—the unglamorous stuff that actually runs your life. A quiet pattern is ready to be unearthed: the schedule that drains you, the habit you've been doing on autopilot, the workload that crept up without you agreeing to it. This isn't the week for a dramatic overhaul. Treat it like a retrograde review—notice what your days are really made of, make one small, private adjustment, and see how it feels by the time Mercury stations direct on the 13th.Moon lesson: Don't rebuild the whole routine—unearth the one habit that's quietly costing you.

Romance, creativity, and pleasure are where this moon plants its seed for you—your fun house. Something you love, or someone you're drawn to, may be asking to be taken more seriously, and the Scorpio energy says keep it close for now. Not every beginning needs an audience. If an old hurt around being overlooked or having to enjoy things alone surfaces, let it inform you without letting it run the show. A creative project started privately during this moon can grow real roots over the next two weeks.Moon lesson: Start the thing you love in private—it doesn't need witnesses to be real.

Mars is in your sign, squaring this new moon in your house of home, family, and foundations—so for you, the friction is personal. The push to act boldly and be seen is running straight into something at home that needs patience and investigation first: a family dynamic, a living situation, a truth about where you come from. Squaring up won't solve it. Getting curious will. What's been unspoken at home starts surfacing over the next two weeks, and you're better positioned if you've listened before you've performed.Moon lesson: At home, investigate before you make the big, dramatic move.

Your house of communication is where this moon does its digging—the words, messages, and everyday conversations that shape your mindset. Something unsaid is ready to surface: the text you drafted and deleted, the thing you know but haven't told a sibling, a friend, or yourself. Mercury is retrograde in the same territory this moon is working, so treat your first draft of any hard conversation as exactly that—a draft. Write it down privately now, sit with what you actually mean, and send the real version after the 13th.Moon lesson: Write the honest version down now—send it after you've read it twice.

This moon falls in your house of money, income, and self-worth—and Venus, retrograde in your sign, is in a harmonious angle with Mars, which means exposure and justice are working together in your finances. A money truth you've been sensing is ready to be confirmed: what you're owed, what you've been undercharging, where your resources have been going in the dark. Don't make the big financial announcement yet. Quietly gather the numbers over the next two weeks, and make your move when Venus and Mercury station direct on the 13th.Moon lesson: The numbers are coming into the light—collect them before you act on them.

This is your new moon—it lands in your house of self and identity, and it's a personal reset. But Scorpio resets don't happen on a stage. Yours happens in private: a commitment you make to yourself, about yourself, that nobody else needs to approve or even know about yet. With so much being unearthed around you, the most powerful move is deciding who you're becoming underneath it all. Plant that intention quietly on Monday, let the next two weeks show you what it requires, and announce it—if you announce it at all—after the 13th.

Moon lesson: Your reset is real before it's public—commit to it in private first.

This moon works in your house of rest, endings, and everything that happens behind the scenes. For you, the unearthing this new moon in Scorpio offers is internal: a pattern you've been running without noticing, a grief or resentment that's been operating in the background, a need for rest you've been outrunning. This isn't a moon for launching; it's a moon for clearing. Give yourself actual downtime over the next two weeks, pay attention to what surfaces when you're quiet, and let an old cycle close properly so the next one can start clean.

Moon lesson: What surfaces in the quiet is the assignment—make room to hear it.

Community is your terrain under this moon—it falls in your house of friends, networks, and future goals. The zoom-out message of this moon was written for you: something you've been carrying as a personal disappointment may turn out to be a pattern your whole circle is experiencing, and naming it together is where the leverage is. A group, cause, or long-term goal could quietly reorganize during this moon. Move strategically, keep your counsel small for now, and let alliances form in private before they go public.

Moon lesson: It's not just happening to you—find your people and name it together.

Your career and public image are the focus—this moon lands in your house of public image. Pluto, direct in your sign, ties your personal evolution to the bigger changes moving through the world. Something about your professional direction is being quietly reset, and decorum is your strategy: like the Scorpio-heavy politicians, you don't have to narrate the transformation while you're in it. If a workplace truth surfaces over the next two weeks, let it. Do your investigating, position yourself carefully, and make the public move after the 13th, when the picture is complete.

Moon lesson: You don't have to narrate the transformation—be mid-change in private, move in public later.

This moon opens your house of beliefs, learning, and the bigger picture—and its whole message is about zooming out. A worldview you've held may get quietly revised as new information surfaces over the next two weeks: about the world, about justice, about what you thought was true. Stay curious rather than certain. A course of study, a piece of writing, or a long-held opinion could all be part of the unearthing. Let your understanding be a draft for now—it gets confirmed and sharpened after the 13th.

Moon lesson: Hold your beliefs like a draft—new information is still coming in.

#6525. Robert Pattinson and Suki Waterhouse’s Complete Relationship Timeline

Despite Robert Pattinson’s big-screen career and Suki Waterhouse’s supermodel status, the public doesn’t know much about their relationship. Both of these Brits prefer to keep their private lives out of the public sphere. As their romance continues past the five-year mark and the couple settles into parenthood, here’s a rundown of their secretive story.

Pattinson and Waterhouse were first linked on July 30 when E! obtained photos of the pair kissing in the streets of London. Per the outlet’s report, the two saw a 9 P.M. showing of Mamma Mia! Here We Go Again at Electric Cinema in Notting Hill. They then walked across the street for drinks at SoHo House until 1 A.M.An eyewitness said the couple was open with their affection. “Along the way, they were very close and cuddled and kissed many times,” the source told E! News. “Robert was very affectionate to her and had his arm around her the whole way and Suki reciprocated by holding his hand and kissing it. They were very loved up and close. Robert stroked Suki’s hair and gave her another loving kiss.”

An E! source said the pair was only “casually dating.” Since Pattinson had only recently ended a three-year relationship, “he isn’t looking for anything serious right now.”

The insider did express that the two “are definitely into each other” and are dating while Pattinson is in London filming The King. “Rob likes to have fun when he has breaks in-between filming and him and Suki have a great time together,” the source added.

LaineyGossip disputed breakup rumors that surfaced at the time, sharing that Pattinson had FaceTimed Waterhouse walking home from a London pub in August. Per the outlet’s report, the couple was spotted at Miguel’s concert in Los Angeles.

They each also attended the Toronto International Film Festival for their own projects that month. Pattinson was promoting High Life while Waterhouse walked the carpet for Assassination Nation.

The couple was photographed exiting London club Chiltern Firehouse at 2:15 A.M., seemingly confirming they were still together.

Photos surfaced of the couple leaving a Christmas party on London’s Regent Street. Waterhouse and Pattinson stayed at the party until the early morning hours.

Waterhouse and Pattinson spent her 27th birthday together, photographed leaving her party. A couple weeks later, People ran photos of them holding hands after a run in London.

Pattinson made his first public comments about his relationship with Waterhouse.

The Sunday Times asked Pattinson about Waterhouse, and he responded by asking, “Do I have to [talk about her]?” Then he went into more detail about why he’s so private about his personal life:

“If you let people in, it devalues what love is. If a stranger on the street asked you about your relationship, you’d think it extremely rude. If you put up a wall it ends up better. I can’t understand how someone can walk down the street holding hands, and it’s the same as when I do it and a hundred people are taking your photo. The line between when you’re performing and when you’re not will eventually get washed away, and you’ll go completely mad.”

However, he did tell the outlet that breakups with Kristen Stewart and FKA Twigs didn’t disillusion him to romance with a celebrity. “They were pretty long relationships, not like three months.”

When it came time for Pattinson’s 33rd birthday, he and Waterhouse were photographed at Chateau Marmont. Pattinson’s friend Tom Sturridge was also in attendance for the celebrations, per People.

During a June interview with Grazia, the reporter noted that Waterhouse FaceTimed Pattinson during a photo shoot break.

E! published a picture of Pattinson and Waterhouse strolling through London as they marked one year of dating.

In early September, photographer Sofia Malamute shared a photo of the couple cuddled together, captioned, “Ibiza, 2019.”

After several months of staying out of the public eye, Waterhouse and Pattinson confirmed their relationship was still going strong. The pair was seen leaving Waterhouse’s 27th birthday party in London on January 12, per LaineyGossip.

They celebrated her birthday at London’s Casa Cruz, and attendees included Liv Tyler, Georgia May Jagger, Cara Delevingne, and Ashley Benson.

Pattinson essentially confirmed that he was quarantining with Waterhouse during an interview for GQ’s June cover. According to the article, Pattinson had been sequestered “with his girlfriend” in the London apartment “the Batman folks rented for him” while production on the film was paused.

The couple signaled they were still going strong, two years into their relationship, with a pair of public outings. On July 21, Pattinson and Waterhouse were photographed walking arm-in-arm around London’s Notting Hill.

A source spoke to E! about the sighting, telling the outlet, “They weren’t recognized by anyone and they seemed to be in their own little world as they took a long stroll around the village chatting intently, pointing at properties and laughing together before they arrived at the club. They held hands the whole time or were linking arms and looked very happy.”

The following day, People published another photo of the couple on a walk. An insider told the outlet, “They are very loved-up,” adding, “they haven’t been together that long. But everything seems on the fast track. They are always laughing and smiling at each other.”

The pair’s most PDA-filled photo yet arrived about 12 days after Pattinson was reported to have tested positive for COVID-19, per CBS News. Although the studio never confirmed that report, production on The Batman was “temporarily paused.” It resumed in September, days after Pattinson and Waterhouse’s outing. In the photo, the couple sat on a London park bench with coffees, kissing while their masks were pulled down to their chins.

Pattinson’s recovery apparently only strengthened his relationship. A source told E! that “Rob and Suki have definitely discussed getting engaged but are in no rush. Suki is not pressuring him, and they are both very committed to each other.”

The insider confirmed the couple’s romance is “stronger than ever” after quarantine. “They love being low-key together and have very similar interests,” the source added. “They are truly inseparable and in love.”

Shortly after E! reported the two had discussed getting engaged, Pattinson and Waterhouse were photographed out with Pattinson’s parents in London. The two walked side-by-side behind Pattinson’s mom and dad on November 23. They opted not to show any PDA in front of them or the photographers who captured this outing.

After months out of the limelight, Waterhouse made headlines when she posted a selfie of herself on April 15. Eagle-eyed fans noticed that a photo of her kissing Pattinson was visible in the background.

On April 19, Pattinson and Waterhouse were photographed out in London for the first time in 2021. The two held hands while walking in Notting Hill. Both dressed casually, wearing shorts and hoodies. It served as a rare public signal that a year into quarantine, the couple’s relationship remained strong.

Waterhouse called out the HBO Max Gossip Girl reboot for making a joke at her expense. The joke in question: Teen public relations whiz Luna (Zión Moreno) is trying to talk Zoya (Whitney Peak) into stepping up her influencer game. She says, “When are you going to get it? As far as the press is concerned, he’s R-Patz, and you’re Suki Nobody.”

In a now-deleted series of tweets, Waterhouse responded with the following: “Another day to be reminded that women can also be the patriarchy. Seeing critiques of patriarchy and sexism, then I get name-checked as somebody’s ‘nobody’ girlfriend,” per Glamour.

Some fans compared Waterhouse’s response to Taylor Swift’s tweet about Netflix’s Ginny & Georgia’s joke about her.

“Hey Ginny & Georgia, 2010 called and it wants its lazy, deeply sexist joke back. How about we stop degrading hard working women by defining this horse shit as FuNnY,” she wrote. “Also, @netflix after Miss Americana this outfit doesn’t look cute on you Happy Women’s History Month I guess.”

A source gave E! a rare and brief update on how Waterhouse and Pattinson were doing three years into dating: great, naturally.

“They are very solid in their relationship,” the source said. During the rare public appearances they do together, they’re “always just totally joined at the hip. You can tell he’s completely in love with her,” the source said.

Ahead of the holidays, Waterhouse and Pattinson were photographed on December 8 holding hands in New York City on a winter day date. Pattinson wore a monochrome blue look consisting of a hooded puffer jacket with matching blue pants. Waterhouse chose earth tones, stepping out in a brown Carhartt hat, rose-colored wool coat, and a black Dior cashmere shawl. It was their first time being photographed out together in months.

Pattinson opened up a little about his life with Waterhouse in two interviews during his The Batman press tour.

To GQ, he spoke about her impact on his decision-making—and how she trolled him by talking with a repairman at their place about DC Comics.

Pattinson said Waterhouse was the reason why he changed the location for his GQ interview from the London Zoo to Holland Park. “I was talking to my girlfriend last night and she was, like, ‘You know, people don’t really like zoos.…’” he said. “I’d been thinking about a metaphorical thing. But then I was thinking that’s very wrong, a sad bear walking in circles. I just can’t help it. I’ll do it for every single element, every decision, in my life. What is the worst-case scenario for this decision?”

And with the repairman for their place’s boiler, “The guy came around the other day, and he just randomly started talking about what a DC [Comics] fan he is. And I’m sitting there facing the other direction, and my girlfriend just keeps continuing the conversation with him. And I’m looking at her like: Shut the fuck up!” He laughed. “Why are you doing this to me? She was very entertaining. Just talking to an obsessive fan.”

Pattinson later talked on Jimmy Kimmel Live! about Waterhouse’s emotional reaction watching The Batman and how it made him more terrified of its release. “It was really her reaction that kind of changed the entire thing because I’m pretty sure she’s not normally into watching superhero movies,” he said, via Entertainment Tonight. “And just seeing that it was capturing her attention the entire time and then she held my hand and touched it [to her face] and I could feel a little tear. And I was like, ‘No way!’”

On Friday, May 6, the couple was spotted in Los Angeles after Waterhouse’s show at The Echo. She was touring to promote her new album, I Can’t Let Go. Pattinson was in a baseball cap and mask to keep a low profile. He was wearing a black jacket, gray T-shirt, and a pair of jeans with sneakers. His girlfriend was in jeans and a colorful long-sleeve shirt over a sparkling top. She had on a pair of black boots with a chunky heel.

They walked down the street as Waterhouse spoke into her phone, and Pattinson threw a casual arm around her waist. She responded with an embrace, continuing her conversation as they went.

Pattinson and Waterhouse made their red carpet debut in Giza, Egypt, while attending the Dior fall 2023 menswear show. As the couple posed for the cameras, they giggled and flirted with one another like they were on their first date.

Later that month, on December 28, the couple was seen making their way through JFK like many holiday travelers. Waterhouse had a few bags over her shoulders, but Pattinson was pushing the majority of their luggage from the trip on a cart, with a guitar slung across his back.

Waterhouse and Pattinson started the new year together. People reported that the two threw a New Year’s Eve party at the Moxy Hotel on New York City’s Lower East Side. A source told the outlet, “Rob and Suki had a great time. He had a table in the corner and was laughing a lot. He and Suki were by each other’s side the entire night. It was a fun evening.”

The Times published an interview with Waterhouse, where she spoke more openly about their relationship than ever before. The outlet revealed they live in London together. “I’m shocked that I’m so happy with someone for nearly five years,” Waterhouse said, noting that they don’t really spend long apart.

On whether they give each other acting advice, she said, “Rob definitely isn’t getting advice from me about acting, but of course I’ll try and get him to help me with an audition before he falls asleep on the sofa.”

Communication makes their relationship work, she added: “I’m always incredibly excited when I see his name pop up [on my phone] or even a text, and I think he feels the same about me,” she said. “We’ve always got so much to say, and I find him hilarious.”

The two both grew up in southwest London and marvel over the fact they ended up together, with such similar journeys in the entertainment industry. “We always say that I never, ever would have thought I’d go out with a boy from Barnes, and he didn’t think he’d go out with a girl from Chiswick,” Waterhouse said.

She didn’t address her future plans with Pattinson explicitly but did say generally she hopes to start a family someday. “You have to be like, ‘I’m going be a sitting cow for a bit of time,’ but it’s going to be worth it,” she said of having children. “I can’t wait. I wish you could click your fingers to make it happen.”

Waterhouse appeared in an interview on CBS Mornings to discuss how she prepared to play keyboardist Karen Sirko in the new Amazon Prime Video series Daisy Jones & The Six. It involved lots of practicing that she said Pattinson had to sit through in their new home.

“Did he enjoy that? Yeah, probably not,” she joked about the practice sessions. But she added that he has his own musical abilities—the actor performed two songs on the Twilight soundtrack, with credits for co-writing “Let Me Sign.”

“He’s actually way worse at being annoying about—well, because he’s an amazing pianist and a really great guitarist,” Waterhouse explained. “He’s amazing, honestly.”

He apparently plays his music for her a lot, and she quipped, “He wins the annoying competition.”

Pattinson and Waterhouse made their Met Gala debut, posing on the red carpet alongside each other:

Waterhouse and Pattinson signaled once more that all is going well between them when they were photographed holding hands while out for a walk in New York City on July 30.

On Saturday, October 21, Waterhouse and Pattinson attended the GO Campaign’s annual gala in Los Angeles. Waterhouse wore a sheer burgundy dress that showed her matching bra and underwear beneath, and Pattinson had on a black suit with a black button-down shirt.

Inside, photos showed them at their table with Waterhouse wearing his blazer over her shoulders. The nonprofit GO raises money for orphans worldwide, and Pattinson is one of their ambassadors.

The pair was photographed on a hike in Los Angeles on November 1. She wore a loose navy sweater with gray shorts, while he was in a gray hoodie and shorts.

On Friday, November 10, the couple went on another hike in Los Angeles. The actress wore a cropped black T-shirt and matching leggings with a black baseball cap. Pattinson wore a weighted hiking vest with shorts and a pair of Adidas sneakers.

On November 19, Waterhouse confirmed pregnancy rumors at the time while performing at Mexico’s Corona Festival. In footage shared on social media, the artist appears in a sparkly, form-fitting minidress with her pregnant stomach visible. She told the audience, “I thought I’d wear something sparkly to distract you from something else I’ve got going on... I’m not sure it’s working.” This was both Waterhouse and Pattinson’s first child.

On November 20, Waterhouse made her pregnancy Instagram official with a mirror selfie.

Waterhouse and Pattinson sparked engagement rumors when Waterhouse was photographed wearing a toi et moi diamond ring on her left ring finger. See photos here.

Since revealing her pregnancy, Waterhouse posted several carousels of pictures from that time of her life. A few days before Christmas, she shared photos from what looks like a tropical vacation, standing in a floral string bikini with a scarf wrapped around her head. In another pic, she had on a crop top showing a peek at her midriff and in yet another, she wore a black-and-white shirt and shorts set with a red handkerchief top underneath that revealed her belly.

The next day, she shared a bunch of photos of what looks like her holiday outfit, a gown by Di Petsa, made of a semi-sheer mesh material that created a “wet look” that was sculpted around her torso.

On December 6, they were seen out in New York City with Taylor Swift.

The couple confirmed they welcomed their first child in late March when they were photographed out walking in Los Angeles. Pattinson pushed their baby in a stroller, while Waterhouse appeared visibly not pregnant in a black coat. The pair had not shared their child’s name, birth date, or sex.

Waterhouse shared the first photo of her and Pattinson’s baby on Instagram. She opted not to share any additional details, including the baby’s sex or name. “welcome to the world angel ❤️,” she wrote.

On April 12, Waterhouse performed at the 2024 Coachella Valley Music and Arts Festival and revealed on stage that the new baby is a girl.

“I don’t know if some of you know, but I had some big life changes happen recently, some pretty big events have been going down,” she told the audience. “I love amazing ladies, and I’ve been very lucky to have my own little amazing lady and meet the love of my life.”

That same night, she and Pattinson were seen at the festival together walking around the Empire Polo Field, enjoying the event. The Twilight star wore a yellow graphic T-shirt, a gold chain, gray pants, and a black baseball cap. Waterhouse was dressed in a furry white wrap, shorts, and sheer black tights.

On April 21, Waterhouse and Pattinson were photographed on a walk with their daughter in Los Angeles. Pattinson pushed the stroller, while Waterhouse was beside him in an oversize white T-shirt, gray sweatpants, and a dark gray sweater.

On Friday, May 31, Waterhouse and Pattinson enjoyed a date night at Chateau Marmont in Los Angeles. The model wore a white top and high-waisted jeans under a black leather biker jacket. She carried a black bag with stud details and wore a pair of espadrille loafers. Pattinson wore a graphic print T-shirt and brown leather jacket with black jeans and sneakers.

Later in the month, Pattinson made his way to Paris for the Dior Homme Menswear Spring/Summer 2025 Show. Fans posted a clip of him talking to a reporter about his daughter for the first time.

“[Having a child] makes you feel very old and very young,” he said, adding, “She’s so cute. And you know, I’m amazed by how quickly their personality comes. So even at three months, I’m like, ‘Oh…I can kinda see who she is already.’”

He also shared he only planned to be in Paris for one day so he could return to his family.

Waterhouse spoke to British Vogue about her life with Pattinson and their daughter, along with how the couple met six years before at a games night in L.A. “I was sure that I’d met him a long time ago, but he didn’t think that we had,” she prefaced. They played a game called Werewolf that was “very, very intense. There were lots of ‘big’ characters, real heavy hitters [in the room]. Al Pacino was there. Javier and Penelope were there…and, you know, everyone was really acting.”

She and Pattinson, “I think we both sort of have the same slight uncomfortable-ness [and quickly] started giggling at the absurdity of the whole thing,” she said, adding they “got told off” for being so disruptive. “There was a director that separated us because we were laughing too much.”

They met again “six or seven months” later, Waterhouse said, and that meeting endeared her more to him. She remembered thinking, “I think Rob’s quite funny, I light up when I’m around him. [Living in L.A.] definitely became a lot more fun when I met him.”

She shared they really planned their pregnancy years later: “One day we looked at each other and said, ‘Well, this is as ready as we’re going to be.’”

Pattinson made her a rap playlist for her birth. “He was there with me and like all dads, he was really nervous, but for someone who’s quite an anxious person, he’s been very calm,” she said. “[He’s] the dad I could have hoped for. I mean a dad and his daughter? It’s an actual love story.”

She also shared he isn’t bothered at all by her exes or them reaching out about the music she makes. “He couldn’t really give a shit,” she said. “He’s like, ‘No one’s better than me, so whatever.’” Overall, she called her life with him and their baby her “dream.”

On Friday, August 9, the couple enjoyed a date night at celebrity hotspot Chiltern Firehouse in London. Waterhouse wore a semi-sheer look with a frilled pink top and translucent black pants. She was photographed leaving the venue in a long black coat with fluffy fur lapels. She left her hair down and accessorized with yellow heels. Pattinson was wearing a blue sweatshirt, khaki pants, a black jacket, and a baseball cap and sneakers.

The two parents enjoyed a walk with their daughter on September 24 in Los Angeles. Both wore black and tan outfits. Pattinson was in a dark hoodie and khaki shorts. Waterhouse had on a leather jacket and longer light tan pants. See photos of them here.

The couple made their first official appearance together since welcoming their daughter on October 5 at the Veuve Clicquot Polo Classic at Will Rogers State Historic Park. Waterhouse wore a black dress with a floral pattern, puffed sleeves, and a belted waist. Pattinson was in a blue suit and a white button-down shirt. They both wore sunglasses.

On Thanksgiving weekend, Waterhouse and Pattinson were photographed walking with their daughter in a carriage outside La Poubelle restaurant in Los Angeles, holding coffee cups.

The model was wearing a black hoodie and wide-legged jeans with sunglasses. Pattinson was in a white hoodie and gray cargo pants with a trucker hat and sunglasses.

In May, Pattinson headed to the Cannes Film Festival to promote his new film with Jennifer Lawrence, Die My Love. He made a rare comment about fatherhood on the red carpet, saying, “I think, in the most unexpected ways, having a baby gives you the biggest trove of energy and inspiration afterward. It’s a different kind of energy.”

He added, “Ever since she was born, it’s reinvigorated the way I approach work, and yeah, you’re a completely different person the next day.”

On Memorial Day weekend, he was back in Los Angeles and seen pushing his daughter’s stroller down the street after grabbing a cup of coffee.

On November 1, Waterhouse joined Pattinson on the red carpet, marking a very rare public appearance together since welcoming their daughter. The couple posed together at the New York premiere of Pattinson’s new film, Die My Love, at AMC Lincoln Center Theater.

They shared a sweet moment in front of photographers and were seen later walking together after the screening.

In an interview with GQ, Pattinson admitted that before he became a dad, he “wasn’t the biggest fan of kids.”

“I didn’t mind them. I would tolerate them,” he shared, saying that now being with his daughter is “the most fun thing. I think it’s absolutely wonderful.”

“It’s just that everything is time management, the whole time. I mean, it’s kind of obvious, but you don’t realize it until you do it,” he continued. “Even if you’re on the other side of the planet, you’re like, ‘Okay, I cannot spend more than 10 days away.’ After 10 days of being away, it’s physical pain. It’s so interesting, your body chemistry changes without you even thinking about it.”

He was then asked if she had watched his movies, and Pattinson stated she has “seen so many” of his and Waterhouse’s films, joking she was a fan of Mickey-17 over popular kids’ cartoon Cocomelon.

He then joked that he is “not getting any respect.”

“I’ll be like, ‘Who’s this? Who’s that on the screen?’ And she’s like…[blank stare]. And I’m like, ‘It begins with a D! Ends with a Y!’” he laughed.

On March 15, Waterhouse and Pattinson stepped out for a date night at the Vanity Fair Oscar Party in Los Angeles. Pattinson wore a black Dior suit, while Waterhouse opted for an ivory Tamara Ralph gown with a sheer cape and embellished bodice.

Days later on March 17, Waterhouse joined Pattinson at The Drama’s Los Angeles premiere. Pattinson was in Dior, while Waterhouse wore a Harris Reed dress.

In a May 28 interview with Variety, the actress implied she and Pattinson are considering more kids eventually.

“I feel like I’m in it for the long run,” Waterhouse shared. “I just want to keep creating, really, and maybe have a larger family…like max two more kids. That would be cool.”

During a July 28 appearance on the And The Writer Is... podcast, Waterhouse shared a glimpse into family life, revealing the nickname their daughter gave Pattinson as he films The Batman Part II.

Waterhouse said that their 2-year-old has started recognizing both of her parents’ careers. “She like knows what I do now,” the singer said. “She like points it out in a story book. We were looking at jobs the other day, and she was like, ‘That’s your job, like the girl with the guitar.’”

She added that their daughter has also embraced Pattinson’s latest role, saying, “She calls him ‘Daddy Batman’ now because he’s always dressed up like that now for the next seven months whenever he’s on FaceTime.”

On September 5, Waterhouse joined Pattinson at the premiere of Primetime, marking their first-ever appearance together at the Venice Film Festival. The actress arrived in a Saint Laurent two-piece gold lace set, while Pattinson stood out in a striped white Dior suit. They posed together for photographers:

In an interview with The Times, Waterhouse said that her wedding plans were on hold “at least until this year is over.”

“It would either be all or nothing,” she said, via People. “If we were going to go for it, we’d have a massive party, blow it out.”

On November 2 at the 2026 CFDA Fashion Awards, Waterhouse told E! News that she’s already looking forward to Christmas with Pattinson and their daughter.

“The tradition I’m most looking forward to is just dressing the tree,” she said, before adding that she’s “excited to go back to London and start drinking a lot of mulled wine.” She explained that she, in fact, makes her own mulled wine and gifts it to loved ones. “I go big at Christmas. I’m excited.”

#6524. Soho House’s New Tokyo Outpost Is a Maximalist, East-Meets-West Wonder

When the Soho House team first began considering their first-ever Japanese property in 2019, one challenge stood out above all—given their hybrid members’ club with rooms model, the hospitality brand’s Tokyo outpost would need to be all things to all people.

For long-time members touching down in the Japanese capital, it had to deliver a genuine sense of place, immersing them in the city’s creative scene and offering a taste of the local cuisine. For Tokyoites, meanwhile—especially those of an Anglophile persuasion, given Japan’s long-standing reverence for British tailoring, subcultures, and craft—the appeal lay in the opposite direction. With the wealth of exceptional Japanese restaurants and bars already on their doorstep, they’d be looking for a slice of that louche, convivial London clubbiness (and possibly a Sunday roast). On top of that, private members’ clubs are still a relatively foreign concept in Tokyo: the few equivalents that do exist tend to skew more corporate.

It was a tricky square to circle, but if Soho House Tokyo—which opened its doors this summer in the design-forward neighborhood of Aoyama, just a stone’s throw from the frenetic energy of Omotesando crossing—is anything to go by, they’ve pulled it off. Credit belongs in large part to Soho House design director Domhnall Nolan, a self-professed Japan obsessive whose six-year odyssey began before the pandemic hit and involved years of traveling back and forth to study the country’s vernacular architecture, interiors, and craft traditions. “One key thing we honed in on was Soho House being inherently maximalist and Japan having a reputation for minimalism—with Tokyo specifically having that contrast,” Nolan explains. “It’s a city of juxtaposition where you have beautiful moments of calm, and then it’s also extremely dense and chaotic. Everything we were doing was always thinking about that juxtaposition of a minimal detail, but a maximal execution.”

When I arrived a few months back straight off a long-haul morning flight, my brain was still sputtering through the fug of jetlag—though the friendly, laid-back welcome certainly took the edge off. Stepping through the discreet timber double doors off Minami-Aoyama, I discovered a moody, amber-lit reception space wrapped in gridded panels of handmade washi paper and a smart check-in desk swathed in glossy Kyoto lacquer. (Even the staff looked almost absurdly sharp, outfitted in custom Japanese denim uniforms created in collaboration with Onitsuka Tiger; at first glance, they may appear intimidatingly cool, but they’re universally lovely and excited to offer tips for what to check out in the surrounding neighborhood.) The mood, both in the design and the general philosophy, is delightfully irreverent: one corner houses a custom graphic-wrapped Japanese vending machine dispensing striped beach towels, while the walls feature tongue-in-cheek artworks painted to look like oversized Uniqlo and convenience-store receipts. If high design is treated as something of a religion in Tokyo, Nolan clearly wasn’t afraid to commit a little heresy.

From there, I headed up to my bedroom—an “Extra Large” that felt like stepping into the apartment of a well-traveled Tokyo art collector. Passing along corridors lined with further custom washi paper, this time in a shade of indigo inspired by Japanese denim, the doors opened onto a living and dining area bathed in a soothing matcha palette and framed by a wraparound balcony overlooking the Aoyama skyline. (Every single room has a balcony, it turns out—a real rarity here.) The devil is in the details: on a crimson-stained credenza sat a row of Japanese spirits, a cocktail shaker, a ceramic sake set—and, in a delightfully retro touch, a rotary phone. Moving through to the bedroom, a timber bed was dressed with a fringed throw woven from upcycled vintage kimono fabrics in the traditional sakiori style, while the sprawling bathroom featured slabs of striated green marble, speckled Nagoya floor tiles, and a freestanding tub stocked with Cowshed bath salts. Even more thoughtfully, a trio of herbal Ross J. Barr patches had been left out on the table, a lifesaver after my 14-hour flight—I reached for the Sleep variety, stuck them behind my ears, and collapsed onto the immaculate cotton sheets.

That attention to local design extends well beyond the headline suites, however; even the “Cosy” rooms are packed with craft details that are rich with backstory. Nolan tells me later that while putting together a mock-up bedroom back in 2023, he spotted a traditional Japanese jewelry box whose dappled lacquer finish caught his eye, which led him to Makino Urushi, a small family-run workshop in Kyoto. “We went to see their factory, which is a handful of people doing everything themselves,” Nolan recalls. “They have a base of three standard colors—black, gold, and red—and when they show you how they create the other shades, you see the incredible depths of color they get. At one point, someone suggested we could make it cheaper in China, and I said, ‘I’m not going to China to make a Japanese finish.’” That persistence paid off: those intricate dappled lacquer finishes now grace mirror frames and drawer fronts, alongside parquet flooring laid in an interlocking tatami-mat grid.

Anyway, despite slapping on those herbal Sleep Patches, my body clock remained wholly uncooperative. By around 9 a.m., I was still sitting in bed staring out at the foggy Tokyo skyline like Scarlett Johansson in Lost in Translation. Admitting defeat, I headed upstairs to explore the two club floors on the 13th and 14th levels, connected by a monumental timber spiral staircase. Here, Nolan’s East-meets-West tightrope walk is at its most nimble. The so-called Club Lounge is cocooned in glossy burgundy paneling inspired by traditional lacquerware, offset by vintage European and Japanese mid-century armchairs, shelves of vinyl records, and a ceiling paneled with woven sea-grass wallpaper and authentic tatami border trims. “I knew it wouldn’t be appropriate to put actual tatami flooring on the ceiling,” Nolan notes. “There’s a sensitivity to it that Japanese members appreciate.”

My favorite detail? Over at the bar, traditional ceramic roof tiles have been flipped vertically to clad the front counter in a ripple of glazed olive green—an especially wry, witty touch—while the 14th-floor bar pairs glowing Italian Murano chandeliers with handmade lanterns and a swirling ochre-and-green onyx bar top. It’s a lot, but it all comes together to form a pleasing, surprisingly serene whole.

Eventually settling into a low-slung velvet sofa, I ordered the traditional Japanese breakfast: a wooden tray bearing a flaky fillet of grilled salmon, sweet rolled tamagoyaki, sesame-dressed greens on chunky glazed earthenware, and miso soup in a turned wood cup. (It proved to be merely the opening salvo of an extraordinary culinary lineup across the house, but more on that shortly.)

Sufficiently fueled for the day, it was time to brave Aoyama, one of the most dangerous neighborhoods on earth for anyone with a weakness for archival fashion—a category into which, much to the disappointment of my accountant, I very much fall. The surrounding backstreets are a labyrinth of designer flagships and meticulously organized secondhand boutiques; I spent the afternoon darting between three different outposts of the designer resale shop Kindal before wandering through the nearby Issey Miyake mini-district, where the late designer’s sculptural fashion wonders occupy their own string of gallery-like storefronts. (Issey-san’s designs are also significantly cheaper here than in the West, though the stock available can be a little spotty depending on the time of the month.) Eventually, with my jet-lagged limbs about to give way, I walked into Kuu, a nearby Japanese head spa recommended to me by the front desk staff. There, a therapist subjected my scalp, neck, and shoulders to an hour of steam, warm water halos, and pressure-point massage so relaxing I practically sleepwalked back to my room, before collapsing for a catatonic afternoon nap feeling like a freshly steamed dumpling.

That evening, we reconvened for dinner in the private dining room tucked behind frosted glass pocket doors at the far end of the house brasserie. Interestingly, Nolan had originally envisioned an Asian-led concept for the restaurant before pivoting late in the process. “As we looked at everything we had in the house already, we thought, ‘We need something that’s very not Japanese to balance these things out,’” he says. The result is a menu that riffs on British comfort classics using hyper-seasonal Japanese produce: our table groaned under plates of crisp tempura courgette flowers and Yamayuri pork loin glazed in a sweet mead reduction, alongside silver cups of French fries and rounds of spicy Picantes. For pudding, slices of tart topped with jewel-like arrangements of green muscat grapes arrived, alongside coupes of soft-serve ice cream crowned with white miso-infused popcorn—an unpretentious and fabulously umami-rich triumph.

The following morning required an even more brutal wake-up call: a 4:20 a.m. departure for Toyosu Fish Market (an hour that Soho House regulars usually meet on the way to bed, not breakfast) accompanied by Soho House Tokyo’s tuna supplier for backstage access to the morning’s bluefin auction. Pulling up to the recently modernized market complex under a drizzly dawn, we were led through a series of Backrooms-esque corridors before finding ourselves right next to the auction floor, watching dozens of frosted bluefin carcasses lined up on wooden pallets under the fluorescent lights. Buyers in rubber boots moved briskly between the rows, using hooks and flashlights to inspect the fat marbling and ruby-red sheen of each tail cross-section before the rapid-fire hand-signal bidding began. Afterward, we ducked into the wholesale stalls to watch a crew wield sword-length knives to break down the colossal tuna loins with surgical precision—and this exact supply chain made its way onto Chef Shinohara’s sushi counter back at Aoyama hours later, where we enjoyed the tuna with freshly grated Shizuoka wasabi and several pitchers of chilled sake.

After lunch, I spent my final afternoon scoping out the wellness and rooftop spaces. Down on the 13th floor, the dual-zone wellness studio—a jewel box of copper-toned walls, carved timber, and a hand-painted gold ceiling—was in full swing; while the rest of my group admirably threw themselves into a dynamic Reformer Pilates session, after a 4 a.m. fish market excursion, I opted to admire the bespoke leather kettlebells strictly as decorative objects, matcha in hand. Instead, I headed out to the 4,000-square-foot rooftop terrace, where the real showstopper—an infinity-style pool tiled in a geometric grid of bespoke ceramic tiles—looked across the sprawling skyline toward Tokyo Tower. (On a clear day, you can even spot the snow-dusted silhouette of Mount Fuji.)

Sitting by that indigo-tiled rooftop pool as the late-afternoon sun dipped behind the high-rises, my Lost in Translation malaise had been entirely dispelled. In a city that can make even the most seasoned traveler feel like an outsider, Soho House has pulled off something pretty remarkable: a space that honors the rigor of Japanese craft while wrapping you in the heady and ever-so-slightly unruly embrace of a great London club. Another shiso Picante, please.

#6522. Inside the NYC Members' Club Where Republicans and Democrats Party Together

A half-dozen of us are squeezed into a small service elevator, our various colognes clashing with the signature fish-and-rubber scent of Lower Manhattan. The elevator operator blares Chinese ballads, and the young man next to me bobs his head in appreciation. An older man shifts uncomfortably. “Could you actually make it louder?” he snarks. Over the course of one excruciatingly slow ride to the sixth floor, we’re trapped in our private discomfort or pleasure. But we’re all headed to the same place: a midterms watch party at The Bench, a members’ club for people who are into politics but feel like political outsiders. It’s a place, according to its website, where “restless organizers, creatives, misfits, sneakerheads, and policy nerds collide.”

Since its founding two years ago, The Bench has hosted insiders ranging from CBS News editor-in-chief Bari Weiss to New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. Monthly dues, “just to keep the lights on,” run as little as $50. The space is regularly used for events unaffiliated with The Bench: readings by literary magazines, climate week pop-ups, splashy debates. Michka Bengio, the social club’s owner and co-founder, is an earnest believer in dialogue and, if his programming is any indication, a little bit of a chaos agent. He likes to produce scenarios that underscore political tensions, like when he had Weiss’s The Free Press, co-host a watch party for Mamdani’s 2025 election. According to those who attended, it was a somber evening for the pro-Cuomo crowd, though some of them nevertheless returned to The Bench for this week’s midterms viewing.

On the night of the midterm elections, partygoers had the option of viewing the election results in a spacious, orderly room displaying CNN’s broadcast or in a lounge-y, narrower space screening Fox News’s coverage. In a cozy hallway between the two screens, guests could buy cocktails and popcorn or engage with people whose political views differ from their own—arguably The Bench’s most exclusive offering.

“There’s just a whole splatter of different opinions that come in here,” says David Azoulay, who works with the content agency Fixer Media. “The Free Press, the Manhattan Institute, and then I also get to meet a lot of people who are working in the Democratic space, on the Biden or Kamala Harris campaigns.” Azoulay helped produce events for an “America 250” tour in collaboration with Young America’s Foundation, a conservative youth organization, and has worked with provocateur Ben Shapiro and former Prime Minister Boris Johnson. Though he used to be a registered Democrat, he “grew up” and now identifies as a proud Republican. While Azoulay engaged in a playful back-and-forth with a progressive 21-year-old over what he considers to be the fallacy of socialism, Democratic councilmember Christopher Marte milled about wearing an “I Voted” sticker.

Over the sound of people screaming about the James Talarico-Ken Paxton race, Marte told me he met Bengio 10 years ago through Arena, a New York-based political organization that took off in the wake of the first Trump presidency. “It was all these young people trying to figure out how to get involved in politics. A.O.C. was on the couch, Alessandra Biaggi, all these people who were just curious, post-Trump election,” he says. At the time, Bengio was working as a campaign manager for Michael Basch, a techno-optimistic Democratic NYC mayoral candidate, a gig he secured by asking the only person he knew in politics to introduce them. He’s also worked as a consultant for NBA Africa and managed downtown restaurants like Regina’s Grocery and Miss Lily’s. The Bench is one of four Bengio ventures; he also co-founded the supper club Shtick with his wife, Jacqueline Lobel, and partners with the Hancock Foundation and the Hancock Cafe. On any given event night, he can be found buzzing around the room, excitedly facilitating introductions for his guests.

The son of a Moroccan father and Algerian mother, Bengio grew up in Strasbourg, France. When I ask what motivated him to move to New York in 2001, he deadpans: “Ever heard of the American dream?” More specifically, though, he was jealous of a friend who moved to the States for six months and returned speaking fluent English. “He was the coolest kid,” Bengio says. “And I was like, ‘I want to go to America, too.’ I love basketball,” he says, reorganizing a pile of books so that the edges aligned just so.

Bengio, a first-time voter, is coy about his own politics. Instead, he’s driven by the promise of America “that you can coexist,” he says, and a desire to nurture civil, democratic debate. “I want to be part of the project.”

“We need to really recommit and reaffirm what we mean when we talk about free speech—expression that is unencumbered by political interference in any way, shape, or form,” says Josef Palermo, a former curator at the Kennedy Center who drove up from the nation’s capital to attend this party. Earlier this year, Palermo wrote about the politicization of the Kennedy Center by both the Biden and Trump administrations in an article for The Atlantic. “We need spaces like this in D.C. Everybody’s in their own camps and certain venues are definitely coded one way or the other. I think having something like this would be huge in our nation’s capital.”

Then again, it’s partly New York’s distance from the D.C. swamp that makes talking about politics at The Bench feel cool. The space is decorated with Bengio’s enviable collection of NBA and political memorabilia. (He jokes that he stays up late scrolling vintage sites and bidding on Americana rarities.) Alongside Michael Jordan Wheaties boxes and a slew of rare basketball sneakers, there’s a framed copy of Emile Zola’s 1897 letter to the French youth during the Dreyfus affair, a portable Florida voting booth from the Bush vs. Gore election, a framed paper shift dress from Richard Nixon’s 1968 presidential campaign, and nearly every issue of John F. Kennedy Jr’s George magazine. The one with a Donald Trump cover gets taken down from the wall often, Bengio says, but he always puts it back up.

On Tuesday night, there appeared to be other collectors of rare political merch. Vintage Obama-era crop tops caught my eye, and a speechwriter for a New York City council member waxed poetic about his favorite vinyl record: a collection of John F. Kennedy speeches. Two guys wore t-shirts they designed themselves that cheekily quoted Michigan turncoat Haley Stevens: “Israel cums to me in my dreams.” (One of them requested anonymity, fearful of being cancelled by the Canary Mission, an anonymous organization that tracks critics of Israel.)

A good number of attendees who were professionally invested in the election outcomes couldn’t stop checking their phones. Anthony DiMieri, the man behind Mamdani’s winning social media strategy, told me he’d just come from Brad Lander’s party. Max Altman, the brother of the OpenAI founder Sam, also stopped by. He’s excited about a recent move to New York from Austin, Texas, and if he hadn’t forgotten to request an absentee ballot, he says, he would’ve voted for James Talarico.

As the results turned progressively blue, the room began to clear out. Before leaving, I chatted with Azoulay’s “libertarian friend” Hunt Beaty. In the hallway between broadcasts, Beaty tells me he’s not terribly moved by the midterms. “Everything interesting that is happening in the world right now, to me, is happening outside of politics,” he says. He rejects the libertarian designation and lives by the credo “free minds and free markets,” citing Reason magazine. And yet, Beaty finds that The Bench still has something to offer him.

“It’s fun to be in a room filled with buzzy, interesting people who at least are able to try and talk about ideas, while also being like, ‘Maybe we’re doing coke in the bathroom, too.’ I want there to be a New York City where those things could coexist.”

#6521. Breaking Down the ‘Black Doves’ Season 2 Ending

For all the international stakes of the Black Doves season 2 finale, the tensest moments really came down to family. Can any spy and/or assassin have a family, found or otherwise? Won’t they all have to kill or be killed in the end? Here’s where Helen (Kiera Knightley), Sam (Ben Whishaw), and Reed (Sarah Lancashire) stand at the end of Black Doves season 2.

This season, while Helen starts to wonder that she’s been sidelined as a “spy wife” and abandoned by Reed, Sam has been given a peculiar kill list by an organization called Kestrel. He has to check it off in order to avoid jail time, or worse, but the names all seem to be connected to the Black Doves of old. This leads Sam and Helen to learn more about Reed, their employer. Then, we learn in final episode that the last person on Sam’s list is Reed herself.

The finale drags out the penultimate episode’s cliffhanger at the beginning of the finale. As it turns out, even though Reed was the fourth and final person on Sam’s list, he did not kill her. He turned her in to Patrick (Sam Riley) alive. That was enough to satisfy his contract, pay his debt, keep him out of jail, and destroy the evidence that Patrick has against Helen. Allegedly, that is! I don’t trust him...

Sam then attends the funeral of Jerry (Samuel Barnett), the concierge he was sleeping with and had to murder because of this mess. There is truly no rest for the wicked.

The rival bird-themed agency that Patrick works for easily recruits the rogue Black Dove. She’s anxious to cause chaos again after getting sidelined to a desk gig.

Oh right... there is a political storyline on this show. It’s easy to forget that when most of the action revolves around spies and assassins who don’t necessarily color inside partisan lines. Ultimately, Helen’s husband’s summit didn’t even happen. Kestrel agents attacked the summit in order to kidnap the US Defense envoy Cecille (Neve Campbell), get Helen in a car alone with Wallace, and orchestrate a confrontation between Reed and Katia Chernov at the Black Doves headquarters.

Big twist alert! We learn in the finale that the Alexi Chernov’s wife is Reed’s long lost daughter “Vita” who she abandoned in the Soviet Union. She’s been secretly plotting this for a long time and aims to get back on her mother and expose the Black Doves. Unfortunately, she neither gets her revenge nor lives to try again. The trio of female assassins–Laila, Williams, and Eleanor–arrive to rescue Reed to get her out.

Katia gives Helen an ultimatum: kill the Prime Minister or their children’s nanny Marie, a Black Dove turncoat, will kill them. (We knew that Marie was associated with Reed at the end of season 1... but both I and Wikipedia thought she was her daughter. Egg on our face, eh?) That’s the only way, Katia says, to put an end to all of this. Seems unfair to Wallace, who as far as we know has done nothing wrong, but whatever. Jerry was also an innocent victim this season.

But Helen does not shoot her husband. Instead, she leaves him in a car park and drives away with Sam to rescue their twins while the other assassins are saving Reed. She does so with a decent amount of ease. Helen shoots Marie point-blank in the head, but then takes her children to safety.

The final episode certainly has its casualties. Katia kills Cecille, sure. I’ve already mentioned that Marie dies, and Katia as well. Dani also dies by grenade in an elevator. But more main characters survived than you may have expected.

At the end of the episode, Patrick stages a meet-cute with Helen and slips her his business card. It’s absolutely a threat. But Reed and Helen are reunited. She also sits down with Wallace and prepares to tell him some version of the truth.

How will he take it? Will Helen and Reed manage to use their skills for good? And will Sam manage to stay in Italy for good this time? Just about all of his friends have contracts to kill him... but what if they just ignore them for a while? Will Eleanor and Williams stay together? We’re going to need Black Doves season 3 to find out.

The two stars had known each other before, but according to the source, they became closer after attending Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce’s wedding in July.

Since then, Johnson has watched Kelly walk the runway in Milan, and sources have shared more about how their connection developed.

Below, everything we know about Johnson and Kelly’s rumored relationship so far.

Johnson and Kelly both attended Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce’s July 3 wedding at Madison Square Garden in New York City.

The two stars already knew each other, but a source close to Kelly told People in September that they “hit it off” at the wedding.

On September 28, a source gave Entertainment Tonight similar intel, telling the outlet that Johnson and Kelly “really connected at Taylor and Travis’s wedding.”

On September 12, Johnson and Kelly were photographed together in New York City, getting out of the same SUV and entering Swift’s Tribeca apartment.

Four days later, a source close to Kelly told People that Kelly and Johnson “have been hanging out and seeing each other under the radar for months now.”

The source explained that Johnson and Kelly “started off as friends and were texting often, but now they’re spending more time together.”

On November 3, Kelly and Johnson were photographed leaving a restaurant in Calabasas, California, after a dinner date. They were smiling and talking to each other in the shots.

On November 5, Johnson and Kelly stepped out for another evening together in Los Angeles, attending a Khaite dinner at Dan Tana’s in West Hollywood. Kelly opted for a more casual look, wearing a green satin bomber jacket over a yellow hoodie and gray sweatpants.

#6518. The Best Dressed Celebrities at the LACMA Art + Film Gala

From Nicole Kidman in Chanel to Anya Taylor-Joy in vintage Pierre Cardin

Last night, a glamorous cross section of the art, film, fashion, and entertainment industries gathered at Los Angeles County Museum of Art for its annual Art + Film gala, which fundraises for the museum’s film initiatives, exhibitions, acquisitions, and educational programs.

This year’s guests decided to embrace a bit of play with their looks. The event is sponsored by Gucci; so fittingly we saw a lot of the brand on the red carpet. Rosie Huntington-Whiteley, who walked in the Spring 2027 show, embraced drama in a slinky, backless black gown with a slit not at the front, but up the back to reveal just a bit of bum cheek. When Demna spoke about this collection this past fashion month, he said he was most proud of the structural feats of his jersey dresses, light as air but engineered to hang just so. Whiteley walked the show alongside additional LACMA guests including Alex Consani, in a dramatically twisted full-skirted gown, Elsa Hosk, who wore a gray wool gown with a thigh-high slit, and Candice Swanepoel in a dress with full-length silver fringe and slits up to her hips.

Anya Taylor-Joy, styled by Law Roach, pulled from the Pierre Cardin archives, selecting a embroidered silvery-white slip with a ruffled organza evening coat. Kylie Jenner wore a look from couturier of the moment, Ashi Studios, that featured a halter neck gown with an allover deer-like animal print and an oversize tassel at the back. And Julia Garner wore a sculptural black taffeta gown from Loewe, which she paired with oversized earrings from Lisa Eisner.

Perhaps the most fitting look of the evening, Nicole Kidman pulled a much-talked-about dress from Chanel’s Spring 2027 collection by Matthieu Blazy. The look features a bodice designed to resemble burlap and a layered tulle skirt with darker panels added to create the appearance of age and wear. It references Degas’ 1881 sculpture “Little Dancer of Fourteen Years,” and is evocative of what this gala celebrates: Kidman, a movie star, in Chanel, one of the most important French fashion houses, in reference to Degas, one of the most renowned impressionist artists.

Ahead, we’ve rounded up our 10 favorite looks of the night.

#6517. All the Wardrobe Essentials Every Guy Should Own in 2026

When it comes to getting dressed, we often rhapsodize about the virtues of “wardrobe essentials for men” as if everyone knows what we mean. So, let's actually talk about it.

On Maslow's hierarchy of menswear needs, wardrobe essentials might begin the perfect white tee, a killer pair of jeans, and the shoes you can wear with them. But in compiling this list, our goal wasn’t simply to meet your needs—you are, frankly, a grown-ass man, and hopefully have those covered—but more to remind you of the fundamental pieces of menswear that have helped men look hotter and feel better for generations. And in a world of non-stop trends, we need these reminders now more than ever.

In aggregate, our essentials constitute the foundation of a rock-solid men’s basic wardrobe. Below, a highly specific starter pack of everything you’ll want—nay, need—to wear in the year of our lord 2026.

A plain white T-shirt can be worn as an undershirt, standalone with some vintage jeans, or—if you want to get DIY—screen-printed into a work of art. Looking for an indie version no one else has? Check out our guide to the best white tees.

Slim, abbreviated trunks or boxer briefs that keep everything in place are the foundation of every rock-solid wardrobe—whether other people can see ‘em or not. Even if you’re in the minority that’s committed to boxer shorts, it pays to spend a little more on something that’s, you know, holding your balls all day long.

We love the zany knitwear options flooding the internet these days. But if we're honest, there will always be a spot in our closets for a classic crewneck sweater. They're timeless and endlessly style-able, even if you only manage to drape one across your shoulders.

There's a reason that the Levi's 501s is at the very top of our guide to the best men's jeans: it has been, is, and always will be the jeans you come back to again (and again, and again). If you dig your denim light and a little looser, though, Gap's Loose Jeans are a close second. Can't think of what to wear? Here's your answer, seven days a week.

If there’s another theme here, it’s that menswear essentials shouldn’t be unitaskers. They should be useful in a variety of situations, and when it comes to tailoring in particular, the navy blazer is a Swiss Army Knife. It works in almost any situation, from job interviews (with a tie) to weddings (someone else's or your own). Bonus points if you opt for a double-breasted number with strong shoulders, brash peak lapels, and an unmistakable sense of what Italians—and menswear guys—call sprezzatura.

The menswear-sphere admittedly overloaded on loafers, and we’re now seeing a slight shift in the shoe zeitgeist. But that doesn’t take away from the fact that the right pair of loafers can still be the most versatile kicks in your closet. They’ve got more range than Daniel Day-Lewis and can go from casual to dressy to punk in a flash. Wear 'em with socks or without, and count yourself lucky when they get truly worn in—then keep wearing them.

Sure, everyone knows a guy who refuses to wear shorts. But he's overpowered every time by his greatest foes: Those months of the year where, honestly, wearing anything but a short becomes a compromise. Our favorite pairs merge style with practicality, and only look better the more thrashed they get. (Except for the Champion shorts—maybe keep those a little cleaner.)

They may have emerged from the sweaty, stylish world of sportswear, but hoodies have long since transcended their athletic origins. These ones have the stamina to take you from a coffee run to casual Friday at the office (just put it under one of those jean jackets we're always telling you about).

We get that simple sneakers aren’t exactly the type of kicks you lust after on StockX, but there’s no denying the rush of dopamine you get when you break out a fresh pair, or how well they go with literally everything. At less than a Benjamin there's the Converse Chuck Taylor, a mainstay of our sneakers coverage, since, uh, always.

Not ready to take the plunge on a serious diver from Rolex or Omega? You're in luck: Seiko's much-heralded 5 series gives you everything you could want in a dive watch—an automatic movement, a day-date display, water resistance, and a near-indestructible case—at a price that won't require a second mortgage. (If you've got a few more dollars to play around with, Hamilton is no slouch, either.)

Like a plain white tee or simple white crew socks, a white Oxford shirt is a true workhorse. It can take the 9-to-5 like a champ, sharpen up for a fancier occasion, or kick back wide open over your favorite vintage tee. If you only have one shirt with buttons, let it be this.

Remember chinos? The wardrobe staple of preppies and, inexplicably, grandpas everywhere? The pant that taps in when your jeans need a break? The ones that Gap viral-ized in the late-90s? These days chinos are back and bigger than before. The chinos of today are surprisingly familiar and look more like the military-issued pairs of the midcentury—high rise and hella roomy. Some even have a pleat or two. We're all for going wide and pleated, but these both present a happy-ish medium.

While people usually start talking about them in April, sunglasses are a year-round necessity—overcast January skies be damned. They’re relevant whether you’re soaking up the summer rays, trying to cut the wintry glare, or simply trying to navigate life with a little more stealth.

Headwear trends come and go—we see you, crochet knit beanies and Trucker hats—but the baseball cap is eternal. You wear one, your dad wears one, your grandpa wears one. The solution for everything from a bad hair day, to an impromptu work Zoom, to forgetting to pack your sunglasses, they're also just plain cool, whether brand new or a little worn out. Always have been, always will.

Sweatpants should be cozy, sure, but the best of the genre are so much more than mere lazy-Sunday garb. We’ve moved past the calf-gripping elastane-pumped versions that have defined the closets of so many Lulu bros and dudes who have skate decks hung up as art. Instead, sweatpants now should be closer to the originals with a baggier fit and even wide-open hems. Spring for a pair that oozes Rocky-level charm, and they'll become the bed-to-bodega bottoms you can't stop wearing outside of the house, too.

There were a few years where the collective menswear consciousness leaned into “fun socks,” and further away from God. How easily we are led astray… Thankfully, we all now agree that the best socks are really the ones you forget that you're wearing, because they're so quietly consistent and comfortable. And in all of our years of reporting on savvy men's style choices, we've never heard a bad word said against any of the four contenders below.

Sometimes clothes can make you feel like you’re living a movie, and a good trench coat is like you’re aiming for an Oscar. (Those trucker jackets with the sewn-in hoodie are more like Hallmark). It’s the most dramatic garment you can have in your closet, and while wooden top coats are great when it's freezing out, a lighter-weight trench coat works the other nine months of the year—and can be paired with a heavy sweater for the other three. You may not be starring in any blockbusters coming up soon, but, boy, will you look like you're ready to.

In cooler temperatures, a reliable flannel shirt is more than a wardrobe essential: it's a no-brainer. Most versions will be plaid, but all of them should feel substantial enough to double as a light jacket, thanks to their lightweight wool or thick cotton make.

It's hard to think of a jacket more useful, more handsome, more versatile—heck, more all three at once—than the canvas jacket. These days, the original designs still retains their utilitarian charm, but the hammer and nails that used to accompany them have long since been replaced by a cell phone and ear buds. And thanks to fashion's ongoing workwear fixation, there's never been a wider range of luxe designer versions available.

Black derbies can pull through when you need shoes for more formal occasions—and also elevate a quick-and-dirty jeans-and-tee outfit. Dr. Martens are a great entry-level choice, and you'll get a lot more mileage out of the Mono pair, which forgoes the brand's signature yellow stitching for discreet black thread.

When your dress pants are this good—roomy and comfortable, statement-making but versatile—there's no sense in saving them for special occasions. Wear them all the time, with anything, the way you would your jeans.

Belts are often an afterthought, but they really shouldn't be. So don't waist (sorry) the opportunity. Much like cowboy boots, the western belt is riding high in fashion right now—but for this story's purposes, we'd like to guide you back to more classic styles, even if the two belts up top have a certain western flair.

By now, you're probably getting the idea that the name of the game here is versatility. While you could opt for Chelsea boots—the right pair will be able to withstand the elements, and any sideways glances from your office nemesis—you'll feel so much calmer in a pair truly designed to stomping through snowy slush.

We love that iconic North Face puffer as much as the next guy (you know the one we're talking about). But don't let its objectively perfect design distract you from the avalanche of stellar, lesser-known alternatives on the market.

A good duffel bag needs to do only one thing: hold stuff. A great duffel bag, though, needs to check off a few more boxes. It should still carry your clothes, kicks, chargers, toiletries, and everything else in the most space-efficient, easy-to-find way possible. But it should also be designed to outlast your passport—or better yet, you—despite years of being stuffed in an overhead bin and thrown in the trunk of your car. We've tested hundreds of 'em over the years, and the ones below offer all that and more.
