#6448. Mussels With Garlicky Miso Broth

Mussels deserve your attention on weeknights. An affordable and accessible protein, they also happen to cook in less time than it takes to boil water. As the bivalves steam, they release a briny liquid, further perfuming the buttery, sake-fortified miso broth. Load up each bowl with a few good ladles, slurping every drop with an assist from crusty bread or warm rice. And why not enjoy the rest of the bottle of sake alongside your meal?

The seafood counter at your supermarket should sell rinsed and debarred mussels, but it’s easy to do at home. Discard any with cracked shells. Gently tap open raw mussels on a counter to see if they slowly close; if they do, those are okay to use. Swish them in a water-filled salad spinner or colander fitted inside a bowl, draining and refilling until water runs clear (give any especially dirty ones a scrub with a sponge). Use a towel to pull off the fibrous beard and set on a towel-lined tray in the fridge until you’re ready to cook.

More seafood dinners this way: Avgolemono Seafood Stew; Spaghetti alle Vongole; and Gorgeous Green Shrimp.

Place 2 Tbsp. scallions from 8 scallions, thinly sliced on a diagonal, in a small bowl and set aside for serving.

Melt 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large pot over medium heat. Add 8 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining scallions to pot and cook, stirring often, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 2 Tbsp. white miso paste and ½ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes (if using) and cook until miso is broken up and incorporated into butter, about 20 seconds. Pour in 1 cup dry sake or dry white wine and stir to combine, then add 3–3½ lb. mussels, scrubbed, debearded. Cover pot and increase heat to medium-high. Cook, shaking pot occasionally, until mussels open, 5–7 minutes (discard any that do not open). Remove pot from heat.

Squeeze 1 lemon half over mussels. Cut remaining 1 lemon half into wedges for serving. Taste broth and season with kosher salt if needed.

Ladle mussels and broth among shallow bowls, then scatter reserved scallions over. Serve with country-style bread or steamed white rice if desired and lemon wedges for squeezing over.

#6447. Turkey Pot Pie

Chicken pot pie is a perfect cozy dinner for chilly fall days, but like most classics, it could use an upgrade. This turkey pot pie is a perfect way to switch up your meal rotation and make sure those Thanksgiving turkey leftovers don’t go to waste. That being said, this dinner is so comforting, it deserves to be made all season long.

What People Are Saying:“This was AMAZING. The filling is delicious, the crust is super flaky and golden brown. I will make this again for sure.” - GoldTeepee

Pop your butter in the freezer for about 15 minutes before you start making the crust so it’s adequately cold. Grab a large food processor and pulse together the flour, sugar, and salt until they’re mixed. Toss in the butter and pulse again until you see pea-sized pieces and larger chunks.

With the motor running, add vinegar and four tablespoons of ice water, one tablespoon at a time, until the dough just comes together and becomes moist. Make sure the dough isn’t wet and sticky or too crumbly (you can test this by squeezing some with your fingers). If the dough is too crumbly and not coming together, add more ice water, 1 teaspoon at a time.

Turn the dough out onto a lightly floured surface and gently squeeze it together. Knead it just a couple of times so it comes together, then split it into two balls. Flatten each one into a smooth disk, wrap them up in plastic, and pop them in the fridge for at least an hour or even overnight if you want to get ahead.

Move your oven rack to the center, then preheat to 375°. Grab a big, deep skillet and melt the butter over medium heat. Toss in the onions and carrots, and stir until they’re soft. Give it about 7 to 8 minutes. Next, add the garlic and cook, stirring, just until it smells amazing (about a minute). Now, grab a spatula or wooden spoon and stir in the flour. Cook, scraping up any tasty bits from the bottom, until the mixture turns golden and starts to bubble—just 2 or 3 minutes.

Pour the wine in slowly, stirring as you go. Let it simmer for about 3 minutes, just until that alcohol smell is gone. Then, slowly add 1 1/3 cups of cream, still scraping up all the good stuff from the bottom. Keep cooking until the mixture starts to boil and thickens up a bit. This should take around 5 minutes.

Fold in the turkey, peas, thyme, and parsley. Give it all a good season with kosher salt and pepper. Take the skillet off the heat and let the filling cool until you’re ready to use it.

Butter up a 9" pie dish or a deep skillet for your crust. On a lightly floured surface, roll out one disk of dough into a circle about 16" across and 1/4" thick. Carefully lay the dough into the pie dish, letting the edges slump down naturally. Trim the dough, leaving roughly a 1" overhang. Finally, pour in the cooled filling.

Roll out the second disk of dough into a 16"-diameter round about 1/4" thick and arrange it on top of the filling. Fold the top overhang into the bottom, pressing firmly to seal. Crimp the edges if you’d like. Using a paring knife, cut slits on top, and brush with the remaining 2 tablespoons of cream and sprinkle with sea salt.

Bake the pie (cover the edges with foil if they start getting too brown) until the crust is golden and the filling is bubbling. This takes about 1 hour 15 minutes. Once it’s done, move the pie to a wire rack and let it cool for about 15 minutes before digging in.

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

Cover your pot pie tightly with plastic wrap or store in an airtight container in the fridge for up to five days after baking. If you’d like to make your pot pie ahead of time and freeze it, wrap the whole (baked or unbaked) turkey pot pie tightly in plastic wrap and store in the freezer for up to 2 months.

#6446. Kylie Jenner Has Called It: It’s Fawn Girl Fall

Kylie Jenner is no deer in the headlights, but she decided to go full fawn at the LACMA Art+Film Gala on Saturday night. Making her debut at the annual Los Angeles event to fundraise for the museum, the beauty mogul joined a starry crowd embracing all things glitzy and gloriously extravagant. For many, that meant a lot of sequins and skin-baring. But for Jenner, that meant a shimmering, body-skimming gown in fashion’s latest animal-print obsession: deer spots.

The dress, from Ashi Studio’s fall 2026 couture collection, was an on-trend departure from the usual leopard and zebra. Cut close to the body in a mottled chocolate-brown and silver fabric that resembled the delicate markings of a fawn, it featured a high halter neckline, a sculpted waist, and a floor-grazing skirt that flared gently from the knees. The original runway design featured tiny, sculptural antlers protruding from the collar, though these appear to have been removed for Jenner’s red-carpet outing.

It was also all business in the front, tassel in the back: the otherwise streamlined gown opened to reveal almost her entire back, with a swirling and shimmering tassel tracing down her spine. It was a little nod to the opulent, old-world glamour currently making its way back into fashion, which has been dominated by luxe detailing: swishing fringe, ornamental frog clasps, oversized bows, and fur-trimmed robes abound right now. More is more, particularly when it comes to the finer details.

Styled by Rose Grandquist and Mackenzie Grandquist, Jenner kept the rest of the look signature sultry. Hairstylist Igor Rosales-Jackson fashioned her jet-black lengths into a glossy, center-parted cascade of voluptuous waves, while makeup artist Ariel Tejada opted for fluttery lashes, softly bronzed cheeks, and a nude-pink lip. Zola Ganzorigt was behind her understated manicure, with jewelry by Lorraine Schwartz adding a final glint.

Jenner is hardly the first to go wild for the print. After years of leopard and zebra reigning supreme, fashion’s animal kingdom has welcomed a gentler, more woodland-inspired contender. Katie Holmes was an early adopter, stepping out in deer-spotted Tory Burch, while Sofia Richie Grainge gave the pattern her quiet-luxury seal of approval with a jacket and sleeveless maxi dress in the debut collection of her label, SRG. On the runways, the interpretations have been considerably more daring. For spring 2027, LaQuan Smith made Bambi print decidedly grown-up, working it into barely-there minidresses, sculpted jackets, and slinky combinations with flashes of lilac lingerie. Baum und Pferdgarten got in on the action by incorporating the motif into its playful, ballet-inspired collection. Elsewhere, British label Cawley Studio has taken a more heritage-minded approach, offering deer-spotted leather flying jackets and pillbox hats, while Carelli has brought the pattern into the realm of plush, statement-making outerwear.

There’s a surprising amount of versatility to the Bambi print. Where leopard has long carried a certain strain of bombshell bravado (remember the “mob wife” trend of yore?), deer spots feel softer and more romantic. Rendered in caramel and cream shades, it works particularly well with fall’s appetite for textures, suede, shearling, and rich, earthy tones. But, as Kylie Jenner proved, the print can look just as at home under the flashbulbs as it does on a countryside ramble

That was certainly the spirit of the evening. The 2026 LACMA Art+Film Gala red carpet was a veritable parade of shine, sparkle, and high-octane glamour, from Kim Kardashian’s oxblood Gucci sequins to the dramatic cutouts of Rosie Huntington-Whiteley. Jenner’s metallic deer look fit right in. This fall, fashion has a new creature to fawn over.

#6443. Butternut Pasta With Sausage and Dates

Squash and sausage are a heroic autumnal pairing, especially in a weeknight-friendly pasta. Butternut is the easiest squash to source—not to mention easily found peeled and chopped (a blessing for those with more timid knife skills). But other winter squash like acorn or red kuri can stand in as desired. Whichever squash you select, a sharp, heavy chef’s knife is best for breaking down the chunky veg. But to make your life easier, microwave the squash for 1 to 2 minutes. It will slightly soften, making it simpler—and safer—to slice through.

Rigatoni’s ribbed surface and large holes help chunky squash sauce cling and bites of seared sausage and date wedge—opting for a nutty whole wheat variety will only add to this meal’s autumnal earthiness.

More cozy pastas this way: Balsamic Mushroom and Sausage Pasta; Creamy Red Curry Pasta; and Baked Feta Pasta With Green Sauce.

Cook 1 medium butternut squash (1½–2 lb.), peeled, halved, seeds removed, cut into 1" pieces (about 6 cups), in a large pot of boiling salted water until very tender, 12–14 minutes. Using a slotted spoon, transfer squash to a medium bowl. Reduce heat to low, cover pot, and leave on burner to keep warm.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium Dutch oven over medium-high. Add 1 lb. hot or sweet Italian sausage, casings removed, and break up into small pieces with a wooden spoon. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, about 3 minutes. Continue to cook, stirring occasionally, until browned all over and just cooked through, 3–4 minutes more. Transfer to a plate with a slotted spoon.

Reduce heat to medium-low. Cook 3½ oz. Medjool dates (about 6), pitted, sliced lengthwise ¾" thick, in same pan, turning halfway though, until deeply browned, 3–4 minutes. Transfer to plate with sausage; season with salt.

Add remaining 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil to pan. Add 6 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and reserved squash. Cook, scraping up browned bits and smashing squash with spoon to break up, until lightly browned and broken up into a chunky paste (pieces do not need to be even), about 5 minutes.

Meanwhile, return cooking liquid in reserved pot to a boil over high heat. Cook 12 oz. short tube pasta (such as rigatoni) until very al dente, about 3 minutes less than package directions (it will finish cooking in sauce). Drain, reserving 3 cups pasta cooking liquid.

Add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid to squash and break up squash with spoon until a saucy consistency. Add pasta, another 1 cup pasta cooking liquid, and reserved sausage and dates. Increase heat to medium-high; cook, adding more pasta cooking liquid as needed, until pasta is al dente and coated in sauce, 2–3 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 1 Tbsp. sherry vinegar or balsamic vinegar. Taste pasta and add more vinegar, salt and/or pepper if needed.

#6441. $22 Fries at Marcel Are One of New York's Finest Little Luxuries

This is Highly Recommend, a column dedicated to what we’re eating, drinking, and buying.

I recently celebrated a dear friend's birthday at Marcel 945 Madison, the much buzzed about restaurant at Sotheby's global headquarters (RIP, old Whitney) on the Upper East Side of New York. Inside the Breuer Building, named for its Brutalist architect, it is a space to behold, equal parts concrete and midcentury walnut accents. Every detail—the luscious lighting, the forged flatware, the tufted mohair banquettes—is exquisitely considered and, likely, for sale.

In this beautiful room full of beautiful people, I could not take my eyes off the frites, priced at $22 under the "Accompagnements" section of the menu in Chroma sans serif type.

Skinny but not shoestring, long, golden, and perfectly salted, they practically glowed from within a napkin-lined bread basket. Every frite was pert, not a single one enervated under a mountain of hot fries. There was no oily outline at the bottom, either.

When I first saw the large portion, I felt a brief wave of doubt: Could we even finish these? How silly of me. We made quick work of the basket, with not a single spud left behind. These fries are so good, they do not need the crutch of a condiment—though they did reach another stratosphere when dipped in plain mayonnaise.

“I like them best with the chicken jus in the roasted chicken dish, or sauce au poivre with the filet de boeuf,” recommends Marie-Aude Rose, chef-partner at Marcel.

When people talk about life's little luxuries, they're talking about these frites. If the best McDonald's fries spent a transformative semester in Paris, they would be a little closer—but still untouchable—to Marcel's frites.

Is $22 pricy? Yes. But we're not talking about a paltry handful landing in a stainless steel cup lined with parchment. These are impeccable, best-in-class wonders, elegantly and generously presented.

I was so in awe that I had to know the deliberate thinking that must be responsible for such perfection. Rose says it is a long process. The kitchen begins with Idaho Russet, chosen not just for taste, but for length and sugar and moisture content that she calls “adequate to frying.”

The potatoes are cut with a French fry cutter, soaked in water, then dried and pre-fried in peanut oil at 160C (320F). During service, they are fried again in clean peanut oil at 180C (356F) and then seasoned with La Baleine fine sea salt, Rose’s salt of choice for seasoning all food at the restaurant.

"Time is important,” Rose said. “You cannot rush cooking.”

Please, chef, take all the time you need.

#6439. Azalea Cocktail

Recipe by Kate McKiernan, Chicago, Illinois

The Azalea cocktail is the signature bright pink, lemonade-and-vodka drink of the Masters Tournament, delivering spring and summer party refreshment.

The Azalea is the signature cocktail of the Masters Tournament, and as a hostess with the mostest, I love leaning into a theme. This drink is a hole-in-one crowd pleaser, whether you’re a golf fan or not. No one can deny the lure of a pretty-in-pink, citrusy vodka cocktail like this one, a perfect sipper on a warm, breezy day on or off the green.

Named for the stunning azalea blooms that famously line the grounds of the 13th hole at the Augusta National Golf Club, the Azalea cocktail is refreshing and perfectly sweet. It’s simple on the page with only a few ingredients, but the bright acid of the lemonade and the sweet kick of the grenadine go perfectly together and work well with a neutral spirit like vodka. It’s an easy cocktail to scale up for a crowd, making it perfect for Masters watch parties, spring brunches or any gatherings that could use a little extra pink charm.

Fill a chilled rocks glass with fresh ice.

Add ice, vodka and grenadine to an empty cocktail shaker. Fill the shaker with ice, and shake the cocktail until it’s well chilled, 15 to 20 seconds.

Editor’s Tip: For a more layered look, add the grenadine directly to the glass and only shake the vodka and lemonade, allowing the pink color to settle to the bottom.

Strain the cocktail into the prepared glass.

Garnish the cocktail with an orange slice and a cocktail cherry.

Editor’s Tip: You can also use the syrup from the cherries to stand in for grenadine in a pinch.

To make Azalea cocktails for a crowd, multiply the portions by the number of people you’re serving. Combine the vodka, lemonade and grenadine in a large pitcher or beverage dispenser ahead of time, then refrigerate the mixture until you’re ready to serve. If you don’t plan to shake each drink individually, you’ll want to add water to the mixture to compensate for the dilution you get from shaking a cocktail over ice. To achieve the proper dilution, add water equal to 20% to 25% the total volume of the base mixture.

Another way to gauge: Make a single serving of your cocktail. Measure the total volume of liquid, stir the mixture with ice until it’s chilled, and measure it again. The difference is the exact amount of water you need to add per serving in your batch.

Stir the mixture well before pouring it over ice, and wait to add garnishes until serving so everything feels fresh.

A rocks glass, aka a double old-fashioned, is the traditional glassware choice for an Azalea cocktail, giving it a classic, country-club feel while keeping things simple and elegant. If you want to dress things up for brunch or spring entertaining, a highball glass also works beautifully, offering extra room for ice and garnishes.

#6438. Oven-Roasted Turkey

The perfect Thanksgiving turkey is easier to make than you might think. Whether you're a first-timer planning a Friendsgiving dinner for your closest pals or the one whose house the whole family gathers at year after year, this recipe will help make your turkey the star of the dinner table. Let this be the year you ace Thanksgiving hosting and find your annual go-to guide for everything—roasting time, thawing, the secret to perfectly browned skin—on how to present the perfect roast bird.

Remove the giblets, trussing, and pop-up thermometers from the turkey. Pat the turkey completely dry inside and out with paper towels. If you plan to cut the wishbone out now, face the turkey neck opening toward you and locate the V-shaped wishbone in the neck cavity. With a sharp and flexible boning knife, using a short but firm swiping motion, gently cut the bone from the breast meat by making long incisions on both sides of the bone. Pry the bone loose with a paper towel or clean kitchen towel and discard. Using your fingers, separate the turkey breast from the skin.

In a spice grinder or mortar and pestle, grind all of the spices until they're finely ground and well combined. This will allow the spices to adhere to the surface of the turkey, especially the dried thyme.

Cover the entire turkey with the seasoning mix, turning the turkey over to season the back as well. Be sure to season under the breast skin and in the cavity. Transfer the turkey to a roasting rack. Refrigerate, uncovered, until cold, at least 12 hours and up to 2 days.

Arrange a rack in the lower third of the oven with no rack above it; preheat to 450°. Gently pat the turkey with paper towels to remove any excess moisture. Place the shallot, lemon, garlic, fresh thyme, and sage in the turkey cavity and neck opening. Be sure not to overfill the turkey. Err on the side of not stuffing everything in if it doesn’t fit. The turkey cavity needs airflow to cook evenly, and blocking that airflow will result in a longer cook time and a drier turkey. Drizzle the turkey with oil. Insert a leave-in probe thermometer (if using) into the turkey thigh or breast and transfer the roasting pan to the oven.

Roast the turkey for 30 minutes. Reduce the oven temperature to 350°. Continue to roast until the temperature in the thickest part of the breast registers 155° and the thigh registers 165°, about 1 hour and 30 minutes more, up to 2 hours more, rotating once during cooking to help the skin brown evenly. Let the turkey rest, uncovered, for 45 minutes before carving.

The full list of ingredients and directions can be found in the recipe below.

Store any leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 4 days. Leftovers can also be frozen. Chill any carved turkey in the refrigerator until cold, then transfer to a freezer-safe bag or container and label it with the contents and date. Store in the deepest part of the freezer for up to 6 months.

#6437. Creamy Miso Mushroom Pasta

Mushroom fans: Bookmark this recipe immediately. It will give you everything you want when you crave a creamy mushroom pasta as soon as the crisp fall air sets in. The hardworking trio of miso, Parmesan, and touch of soy sauce delivers an umami bomb of flavor that doesn’t overwhelm, but magnifies, the best of earthy mushrooms. Coupled with luscious noodles enrobed in a creamy (but not heavy) sauce, what’s not to love?

A few helpful notes for pasta success: (1) While any pasta will work, egg-based noodles, like the fettuccine I recommend here, are the best complement to the sauce. The nests (Rummo and De Cecco are great accessible brands) cook far faster than standard straight pasta, almost as fast as fresh. (2) Don’t be afraid to season your mushrooms! Yes, I know this goes against all that we’ve learned about salting them too early in the cooking process, but just a bit of salt will get them going and releasing their water faster for eventual crisp-browned edges. Don’t be alarmed if you see a pool of water at the start of the mushroom cooking—that’s to be expected and just keep going until it evaporates. (3) Don’t forget to reserve plenty of pasta cooking liquid, which is critical to the eventual sauce’s success. I prefer transferring the al dente noodles from the pasta pot to the skillet, letting any residual water come with it (and to ensure you don’t accidentally drain away that liquid gold).

Find more fall favorite meals here: Weeknight Pumpkin Chili; Cream-ish of Mushroom Soup; Mushrooms au Poivre.

Cook 12 oz. egg-based pasta (such as fettuccine nests) in a large pot of boiling salted water, stirring occasionally, until al dente, about 1 minute less than package directions.

Meanwhile, heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet over high. Add 1 lb. crimini or mixed mushrooms (such as button, maitake, oyster, and/or shiitake), sliced ¼" thick or torn into bite-size pieces, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt and toss to coat evenly. Spread out into an even layer and cook, undisturbed, until mushrooms are starting to release their liquid, 2–3 minutes (do not be alarmed; there will be a lot). Continue to cook, tossing occasionally, until moisture is almost completely evaporated and edges of mushrooms are starting to brown, 6–8 minutes.

Reduce heat to medium-high; add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Cook, tossing often, until garlic is fragrant and golden, 1–2 minutes. Pour in ¾ cup dry white wine, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan with a sturdy spatula or flat-edged wooden spoon, and cook until wine is mostly evaporated (you should have about 1 Tbsp. liquid left in pan), about 4 minutes. Reduce heat to medium-low. Add 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, cut into pieces, and 2 Tbsp. white miso and stir until melted and combined. Slowly pour in ½ cup heavy cream, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan; simmer until thickened slightly, 2–3 minutes. Add 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce; season with freshly ground pepper. Taste and add more salt if needed.

Using tongs, transfer pasta to mushroom mixture and add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid. Increase heat to medium and bring to a simmer. Cook, tossing constantly and adding ½–1 cup more pasta cooking liquid to reach desired sauce consistency if needed, until pasta is al dente and liquid has thickened slightly, about 3 minutes.

Remove pan from heat. Add 1 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about ½ cup) to pasta and toss to combine. Season generously with more pepper; taste and season with more salt if needed.

Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with more Parmesan and pepper.

#6436. Brownie Batter Bark

Recipe by Molly Allen, Hood River, Oregon

This egg-free brownie batter bark is quick and easy, and tastes just like brownie batter straight from the bowl.

When I’m making brownies, I always want to swipe my finger against the edge of the bowl and taste the brownie batter. The problem? While it’s delicious, brownie batter contains raw eggs and raw flour, which can make you sick. When you want to lick the spatula but don’t want to risk food poisoning, this brownie batter bark recipe is the perfect solution.

Line a 15x10x1-inch baking sheet with parchment paper.

In a large bowl, combine almond flour, brown sugar, cocoa powder and salt. Stir in the melted coconut oil and vanilla extract until the mixture is smooth.

Spread the mixture on the prepared baking sheet into an even layer. Freeze it for 20 minutes.

Meanwhile, in a small microwave-safe bowl, microwave 1 cup of chocolate chips in 30-second increments until they’re melted, stirring between the intervals. Spread them over the frozen base. Sprinkle the bark with the remaining 1/2 cup of chocolate chips.

Freeze the bark for one hour or until it’s firm. Break it into pieces.

Brownie batter bark is best stored in a zip-top bag or airtight container in the freezer. The cold freezer temperature will keep the bark hard, and provides the best texture when you pull out a few pieces to enjoy. Keep the bark stored in the freezer for up to two months.

This is a great make-ahead potluck dessert. Make it any time, and then store it in the freezer. Grab a few pieces at a time, or serve a whole platter to a crowd.

No almond flour on hand? You can swap in all-purpose flour, but keep in mind the texture may not be the same. If you use all-purpose flour, it should be heat treated before consuming raw.

Spread the flour on a baking sheet and heat it in a 400ºF oven for about five minutes or until it reaches an internal temperature of 160º. Then add it to the dry ingredient mixture.

This recipe calls for unsweetened cocoa powder to deliver deep chocolate flavor. Semisweet chocolate chips are used for the melted chocolate topping for a balance of sweetness. It’s best to stick with semisweet chocolate for a more robust flavor (as opposed to milk chocolate).

You can melt chocolate either in the microwave or over a double-boiler on the stove top. Heat the chocolate slowly on low heat for the smoothest consistency.

#6432. Think You Don’t Like Broccoli Rabe? You’re Cooking It Wrong

BA’s Best is our vault of the Test Kitchen’s definitive takes on iconic dishes. Today, food director Chris Morocco breaks down his latest recipe, a restaurant-worthy pasta dish you can pull off on a weeknight.

I didn’t grow up with southern Italian dishes like orecchiette with sausage and broccoli rabe, most likely because it originates in Puglia, a region close to my grandmother’s Campania. Her mistrust of the Pugliese, the home province of many of her neighbors in Worcester, MA, was infamous in our family. “Horse eaters” she would whisper, and flick her curtains closed.

Yet this is one of the easiest foundational Italian dishes to make, in a matter of minutes with some basic ingredients. It is balanced in a way that few other pastas could hope for, containing an abundance of greens to counter punchy sausage and handfuls of Parmesan.

Shockingly, Bon Appétit didn’t have a classic recipe for it. That is, until now. I got to work in the Test Kitchen—here are my big takeaways.

Too much ink has been spilled trying to convince home cooks that there are definitive pairings between sauces and pasta shapes. I don’t think your amatriciana gives a hoot if you use strozzapreti or gemelli. Yet I can’t deny the charms of orecchiette for this dish, as the “little ears” are perfectly sized and shaped to cradle nubbins of sausage, and be swaddled by clingy leaves of broccoli rabe. Any short shape will play nicely with the other elements—mezzi rigatoni and lumache especially. Be sure to leave the pasta very al dente before draining, since it will continue cooking with the greens and sausage.

Blanching—a brief dip into simmering salted water—isn’t nearly assertive enough to tame the fibrous stalks of broccoli rabe. To get them truly silky and tender, I give the bottom half of the stalks a 5-minute head start in boiling water, followed by 5-ish more minutes with the tops. There’s no need to shock in ice water or cold water afterward. These fully cooked greens are so luscious, they function almost like a sauce, with some help from cooking liquid and butter.

Italian-style sausage has the sharp scent of fennel, lots of garlic and black pepper, and, in hot varieties, red pepper flakes. If you can find it loose, great, but generally, you will have to remove the casings yourself to reveal the coarsely ground meat. This coarse grind is another key aspect to the dish, as it results in pebble-size chunks that render and crisp without turning into paste.

For years I undercooked my broccoli rabe, barely blanching it to temper some bitterness, yet leaving it so fibrous that even a longer cook with the sausage could never fully unlock its silky potential. I know better now. My colleagues in the Test Kitchen were floored by how delicious an overcooked vegetable can be—how the rabe became creamy like a green sauce, tangling around every other ingredient. It’s not every day you find a dish that you can make just as well as what you might order in a restaurant, after a long work day no less. But this is one of them.

#6431. Cider-Braised Sausage and Lentils

I haven’t made a meal in the French countryside in fall; but sometimes I dream, and these slow-cooked lentils are what I’d make in such a situation. Back in my American reality, it still makes an excellent dinner or hearty weekend lunch. Look for mild smoked Austrian or German sausages, which lean on mellow herbs and warm spices (sometimes, if you’re lucky, they’re also stuffed with a nutty cheese)—this style is already cooked to a safe temperature, but the casing’s texture is greatly improved when seared before reheating. If your shop only carries sweet Italian sausage or something like an apple-stuffed chicken sausage, both work in a pinch. What a treat it will be to actually finish off that gallon of apple cider you impulsively bought last week in the lentil-braising liquid.

More great fall recipes this way: Charred Cabbage With Sausages and Apples; Pork Chops With Green Chiles and Apples; Mustardy Cider-Braised Pork Chops.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium heavy pot over medium-high. Cook 6–8 smoked Austrian or German sausages (1–1½ lb.), turning often, until deeply browned on all sides, about 4 minutes. Transfer to a plate.

Combine 1 large red or yellow onion, finely chopped, 3 celery stalks, finely chopped, 1 large carrot, peeled, finely chopped, 1 tsp. freshly ground pepper, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in same pan. Reduce heat to medium and cook, stirring often and scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan, until vegetables are softened, 6–8 minutes. Add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and cook, stirring, just until fragrant, about 1 minute.

Add 2 cups low-sodium chicken or vegetable broth, 1½ cups apple cider, 1½ cups French green lentils, picked through, rinsed, ½ cup finely chopped parsley, 3 Tbsp. Dijon or whole grain mustard, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt to pan. Increase heat to high and bring to a boil. Cook until liquid is slightly reduced, about 5 minutes. Cover pan, reduce heat to medium-low, and cook until lentils are tender and most of the liquid is absorbed but mixture is still saucy, 30–35 minutes.

Uncover pan and stir in 1 Tbsp. apple cider vinegar or red wine vinegar. Nestle sausages into lentil mixture and add any juices pooled on plate. Simmer until sausages are warmed through, about 5 minutes. Top with parsley leaves and reserved celery leaves to serve.

#6429. We Tried Every Boxed Stuffing We Could Find—These Are The Only Ones We’d Buy Again

Some mixes taste so homemade, they just might fool your Thanksgiving guests.

In my opinion, stuffing is the crème de la crème of a Thanksgiving feast. I’d choose it over any other carb or veggie side. Everyone knows stuffing balances a buttery, crispy top with a moist, tender interior and subtle aromatics. It should be the greatest complement to a turkey. But sometimes we can’t get around to making a homemade stuffing on Thanksgiving, so we settle for a box mix.

We tried a variety of stuffings so you don’t have to wonder which one to pick up at the grocery store. We were looking for stuffing that could be mistaken for homemade, with a balanced texture and real seasoning. We tried eight stuffings, but only five were worthy of adding to your holiday table or weeknight rotation.

This ShopRite stuffing is super weeknight-friendly, and I wouldn’t hesitate to make this for an easy dinner side. Because it’s made with chicken broth, you can use water to make it without losing too much flavor.

This Pepperidge Farm Stuffing was the most surprising one I tried. Because it contains whole wheat and therefore is a little darker in color, I wasn’t sure I would like it. The flavor was excellent, though, and I really appreciated the homemade feel of having to add your own fresh chopped onion and celery.

It's admittedly been years since I had my end-all, be-all favorite boxed stuffing as a kid, Stovetop’s Savory Herbs. And you know what? It really holds up.

As the name suggests, this boxed stuffing mix is Big-S Savory and loaded with herbs, with a buttery, peppery backbone. It gets perfectly crispy around the edges. It’s both nostalgic-good and delicious enough to keep a box on hand for after Turkey Day, if not just to make these sausage stuffing bites.

Here is where the fooling comes in, with Kinder's Brown Butter & Herbs Stuffing Mix. One bite of this garlicky, nutty stuffing had me say out loud, “Oh, this is deluxe.”

Not only that, but this might be the easiest stuffing of them all, with no fewer than three different ways to prepare and serve it. There’s a sausage-spiked version, a skillet-made version, and an ultra-savory version with leeks. In short, if you're really in the mood for a homemade stuffing experience, but you're running out of prep time, Kinder's stuffing will trick everyone into thinking you made this fully on your own.

While Kinder’s is great when you still want to eat like a Thanksgiving maximalist, some of us want the easiest (but no less delicious) route. In which case, Mrs. Cubbison’s Traditional Stuffing will take you there.

I’ve long been a fan of the brand’s herby, buttery croutons, so I’m not surprised that Mrs. Cubbison’s Traditional Stuffing is yet another one of its products I'll always keep on hand. The bread base is just the right amount of toasted and caramelized, making for a stuffing that's tender and crispy around the edges (no mush here). Plus, it'll even free up some space in your oven since it can be made in the slow cooker, too.

#6427. Cut It Out! Hollywood’s Red Carpets Are Finding New Ways to Show Skin

Kim Kardashian has never met a cutout she didn’t like. The reality star and fashion provocateur has made something of a signature out of showing skin in unexpected places—she loves an exposed hip, a plunging neckline, and a dress that appears to defy the laws of physics. At last night’s 2026 LACMA Art+Film Gala in Los Angeles, she was in familiar territory, wearing a burgundy sequined Gucci gown by Demna that was all business from the front, with its high neck, long sleeves, and sculpted silhouette, and decidedly less so from the side. A dramatic slash across the waist revealed an expanse of skin above the hip.

And she was far from alone. If the evening’s red carpet was anything to go by, Hollywood’s appetite for the naked dress has evolved into something more architectural and off-beat. Forget the romantically diaphanous or the all-out sheer, the latest approach to showing skin is all about strategic exposure. Think a dramatically placed opening, a vertiginous slit, and plunging, crack-skimming backs. Sometimes, what a dress conceals is just as important as what it reveals.

Leading the charge, of course, was the cohort of celebrities dressed by Gucci, where Demna has established a provocative, high-octane strain of glamour. Rosie Huntington-Whiteley wore a black, long-sleeved custom gown with exaggerated shoulders and a severe, almost monastic front that gave way to a completely exposed back and butt, with a daring slit extending to the hip, fastened with a small jeweled detail. Restrained from one angle, outrageously risqué from another.

Fellow model Amber Valletta also opted for custom Gucci, in a black column gown with a plunging open back, a silver ornamental detail, and a thigh-baring slit that extended almost to her waist. Emily Ratajkowski chose a white draped Gucci number with a plunging neckline and dramatically open sides, paired with a sky-high leg slit.

There were plenty more variations on the theme. Alix Earle embraced the evening’s maximalist mood in a silver Gucci, disco-ready halter gown dripping with strands of shimmering embellishment, with a thigh-high slit emerging from beneath the metallic fringe. Olympic skier Lindsey Vonn also turned to Gucci, wearing a glittering, one-shouldered purple gown with an asymmetrical neckline and a dramatic slit that revealed a sheer black-stockinged leg. Candice Swanepoel took a similarly sparkling approach in a silver, crystal-strewn gown with a plunging neckline and two daringly high slits, with more sparkle cascading over her legs.

Not everyone was in Gucci, though. Madelaine Petsch opted for a look from Georges Hobeika’s spring 2027 collection, with a black halter-neck bodice that offered a hint of side-boob, and which plunged almost to the waist before meeting a cream floral-embroidered pencil skirt.

The naked dress has long been a Hollywood fixture. Body-conscious designs are beloved by the Kardashian-Jenner clan, having a deep understanding of the impact of a well-placed flash of flesh. But then there’s people like Anya Taylor-Joy, a champion of the sensuous and barely there, keeping a more ghostly and romantic bent with winter-white corsetry by Dilara Findikoglu and forays into vampy Tom Ford. This new iteration, however, uses precision cuts and dramatic contrasts to draw the eye to particular parts of the body.

With Demna’s Gucci helping to usher in a new mood of all-out, unabashed glamour, it seems the red carpet is entering its next undressed era.

#6424. Broiled Salmon Teriyaki

Sometimes all it takes to make dinner feel special is a big, bold piece of protein. Case in point: This salty-sweet salmon glazed in a glossy teriyaki-style sauce. Brushed in two rounds with the quick sauce made with nothing more than sugar, soy sauce, sesame oil, and vinegar, the salmon sizzles under the broiler, charring as it takes on a smoky flavor. This recipe calls for one large piece of salmon, but you can use smaller fillets or opt for a white fish such as cod or halibut. Just note that the cooking time will be shorter if using smaller pieces, so keep an eye on them. Add a quick garnish of sliced scallions and toasted sesame seeds, and dinner is done.

More salmon winners this way: Hot Honey-Glazed Salmon; Green Curry-Glazed Salmon; and Slow-Roasted Salmon With Harissa.

Bring ⅓ cup (packed; 67 g) dark brown sugar, ¼ cup soy sauce, 2 Tbsp. unseasoned rice vinegar, and 2 tsp. toasted sesame oil to a simmer in a small saucepan over medium-high heat; cook until reduced by half and syrupy, 5–7 minutes. Let sauce cool until thickened slightly, about 10 minutes.

Heat broiler (if broiler is in your oven, place rack in upper third). Season both sides of one 1½–2-lb. skinless or skin-on center-cut salmon fillet with kosher salt. Place, skin side down, in a skillet or baking dish. Transfer one third of sauce to a small bowl and set aside for serving. Brush about half of remaining sauce over fillet. (If the salmon has a lot of room around it in the pan, line with foil to prevent runoff sauce from burning onto pan.)

Broil salmon until sauce is just starting to burn in spots, 4–7 minutes. Brush remaining sauce over fillet and broil until deeply charred and salmon is opaque all the way through, about 5 minutes.

Remove fish from oven and spoon reserved sauce over. Top with thinly sliced scallions and/or toasted sesame seeds if desired.

#6422. BA's Best Orecchiette With Sausage and Broccoli Rabe

Unlike many iconic Italian recipes, this luxurious union of silky broccoli rabe, chile-flecked sausage, garlic, and curvaceous pasta is a weeknight hero. You can make it start to finish, in about 30 minutes. The key to successful execution is to go way beyond blanching when it comes to precooking the broccoli rabe in boiling salted water. For tender rabe that melds seamlessly with pasta and sausage, start by separating the thick stems from the rest of the stalks and giving them a head start before adding the rest. It removes any unpleasant bitterness and also means the rabe will cook into the saucy base of browned sausage and sweated garlic in just minutes.

While orecchiette is the traditional pasta choice, any short pasta will work. Sausage has become a popular addition to the true original Pugliese dish of stewed broccoli rabe with pasta, but a tin of anchovies makes a great substitute for added oomph and intensity.

This recipe is one of BA’s Best, our vault of the Test Kitchen's definitive takes on iconic dishes.

Cut 2 large bunches broccoli rabe, trimmed, in half crosswise to separate thick stalks from thinner stems and florets. Cook thicker stalks in a medium pot of boiling salted water until crisp-tender, about 5 minutes. Add thinner stems and florets and cook until all of the broccoli rabe is tender (the tip of a paring knife should slide through the stalks with little to no resistance), about 3 minutes. Transfer to a rimmed baking sheet with tongs; let sit until cool enough to handle (no need to squeeze out excess water unless dripping wet). Coarsely chop into bite-size pieces.

Meanwhile, cook 1 lb. orecchiette (little ear-shaped pasta) or other short pasta in a second medium pot of boiling salted water until al dente (or use same pot with fresh salted water). Drain, reserving 2 cups pasta cooking liquid.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium-high. Cook 1 lb. hot Italian sausage, casings removed if needed, breaking up with a wooden spoon, until golden brown and nearly cooked through, about 5 minutes. Add 1 head of garlic, cloves separated, peeled, thinly sliced, and remaining 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Cook, breaking up sausage even finer if needed and stirring often, until garlic is golden brown and softened, 3–4 minutes. Add broccoli rabe and cook, stirring occasionally, until very tender and wilted, about 5 minutes.

Add 4 Tbsp. (½ stick) unsalted butter, cut into pieces, pasta, and 1 cup pasta cooking liquid. Cook, stirring often and adding more pasta cooking liquid as needed, until pasta is coated in a clingy sauce. Taste and add some crushed red pepper flakes if desired. Add 1 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about ½ cup), and stir, adding more pasta cooking liquid a splash at a time as needed to keep sauce smooth and shiny, until incorporated; season with salt.

Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with more Parmesan.

#6421. Butterball Made a Tiny Turkey That Assigns Thanksgiving Chores—And It’s Free

Turkey, stuffing and a little accountability are on the menu this year.

There’s always that one Thanksgiving guest who says, “Just tell me what to do!” while somehow managing to avoid doing anything. Well, Butterball has a tiny turkey for that.

On Monday, Nov. 2, the turkey brand took to Instagram to introduce the Butterball Buddy, a tiny electronic taskmaster that hands out Thanksgiving chores so the host doesn’t have to. It looks like something straight out of the ’90s, and the best part? It won’t cost you a dime.

As silly as a chore-assigning turkey sounds, the company might be onto something. Its 2026 Togetherness Report found that 85% of Thanksgiving hosts would prefer guests to offer to help, but only 38% ask. Nearly half say the final cleanup is where they could use an extra hand.

Once everyone arrives, guests pass the Buddy around like a hot potato. When it chimes and vibrates, whoever’s holding it gets a task, whether that’s setting the table before dinner or tackling the dishes afterward. Finish the job, pass it along, and it’s the next lucky helper’s turn. Think Tamagotchi, except instead of keeping a digital pet alive, you’re keeping the kitchen from turning into a disaster area.

Set an alarm. The first batch dropped Nov. 2, and two more are coming at 1 p.m. ET on Monday, Nov. 9, and Monday, Nov. 16, at ButterballBuddy.com. Quantities are limited, so the early birds get the turkey. The giveaway is open to legal U.S. residents ages 18 and older, and no purchase is necessary.

The Buddies may be in short supply, but Butterball’s cooking advice isn’t. Its Turkey Talk-Line is celebrating its 45th anniversary this year, with more than 50 experts answering questions about everything from thawing to checking for doneness through Dec. 24. You can call 1-800-BUTTERBALL, text 844-877-3456 or chat live at Butterball.com. The hotline’s contact information is printed on the back of every Buddy, too.

#6419. Urban Lights & Gucci Nights: An Exclusive Look Inside the LACMA Art + Film Gala

The night was young. Very young, as I cruised across Los Angeles to this year’s LACMA Art + Film Gala. I decided to arrive before the usual red-carpet mayhem starts, and because I had gotten ready several hours too early, I was starting to entertain the idea of having a quick nap in my glam and gown. I was wearing a 1930s purple satin bias-cut dress that I won at an auction for considerably less than it was worth. Such a purchase can do wonders for one’s self-esteem: I felt like a million bucks.

This year marked the 15th anniversary of the gala, which honors artists and filmmakers while raising funds to support the museum’s programming. The evening, sponsored by Gucci and co-chaired by Eva Chow and Leonardo DiCaprio, would celebrate Latvian artist Vija Celmins and filmmaker Denis Villeneuve. The art world and Hollywood are not always natural bedfellows, although they have certainly become more comfortable with one another over the years. I was interested to see how the two would behave over dinner.

I arrived fashionably early, both because I am extremely punctual and partly because I have developed an aversion to the chaos that accompanies certain Los Angeles events. Anya Taylor-Joy was making her way towards the photographers in an archival Pierre Cardin sculptural gown and jacket looking like a beautiful futuristic loofah. I spotted the sparkle of her Tiffany & Co. Schlumberger Stars and Moons necklace before I even registered who was wearing it. The necklace was doing its own job of announcing her.

As she approached the carpet, which was lined with photographers and press, I was surprised that nobody was yelling. The atmosphere was remarkably calm, a far cry from some of the movie premiere assignments I’ve attended, where you can barely hear yourself think over the screaming of fans and photographers. Behind the carpet was the backdrop that has become something of a celebrity in its own right: Chris Burden’s Urban Light, the monumental installation made up of more than 200 restored cast-iron antique street lamps. It is a Los Angeles sight that never loses its magic.

In the distance, I heard a woman having a meltdown with security. “Am I not famous enough?” she yelled.

I never established what the issue was. Perhaps she had been denied access to the carpet, or she simply wanted to take a photograph and was being told no. Either way, she was making a scene in sparkles. I hurried past the publicists who were watching with mild horror. “Never a dull moment,” I said. One or two laughed as I continued inside.

During cocktail hour, I stopped to say hello to Ed Ruscha, whom I had met a few nights earlier at a birthday party. He would be seated at Larry Gagosian’s table that evening. I made my way around the room, passing Julia Garner, who is invariably one of the nicest people in it. She was wearing Loewe with sculptural gold earrings. She always asks me if I’m an actress, which makes me blush slightly, despite the fact that I have never once given her reason to believe that I am. Nearby, Iris Law was wearing a beautiful pearlescent tiled dress by a brand she told me was called Amaramara. Up close, the dress looked almost as though it had been constructed from mother-of-pearl shells. She explained that it was lined in leather, making it surprisingly soft against the skin.

I walked by a cluster of familiar faces, getting stepped on a few times along the way—a long train is lovely in theory, but less so in a crowded room full of people who have somewhere to be. I spent much of the evening trying to protect my almost 100-year-old archival satin from people’s shoes. Artist Alex Israel told me he was particularly excited to see Rosé perform later that evening. I spotted Jonas Wood in the distance, along with Lauren Halsey, who had recently created the most extraordinary art direction and stage design for Erykah Badu at the Hollywood Bowl. I had been lucky enough to see it, and Halsey had projected her artwork across the venue, making the entire experience feel as though you had stepped directly into her world.

I also ran into Jordan Firstman, whose film Club Kid had just come out. We heard about a rather unexpected screening, which included Oprah. Apparently, she wasn’t entirely familiar with the film’s more specialized vocabulary and required a brief introduction to gay culture, including what a popper was and what people meant by G. (I would have loved to be there for that.)

Meanwhile, waiters were circulating with bite-sized beef tenderloin and miso black cod. I attempted to be a fly on the wall and observe who was talking to whom. Many of the faces I didn’t recognize were presumably museum patrons. I always find it interesting trying to distinguish between those who are famous and those who are simply very rich. At a gala like this, the two categories overlap quite considerably.

Eventually, bells rang and we were ushered across the museum towards the dining room. On the way, I spotted Jennifer Tilly, whom I am a big fan of. I complimented her Gucci ensemble and told her I admired her JAR jewelry collection. She immediately asked if I wanted a selfie. It turned out to be one of my favorite photographs of the night.

Jennifer told me that her dress had been five sizes too large the evening before, but that the Gucci elves had worked their magic and made it fit just right. She was wearing a Jean Schlumberger Hedges and Flowers necklace for Tiffany & Co., with matching earrings from the 1960s. It is one of his most iconic designs, and she lit up as I asked her about it. I found myself thinking that I would happily abandon the rest of the evening to order a martini with her and gossip. She was delightful.

I also introduced myself to another Real Housewife I have a soft spot for, Kathy Hilton, who told me she was wearing vintage Gucci. The bow at her collar looked Edwardian-inspired.

The dining room was arranged with extraordinarily long tables with crisp white tablecloths and florals, giving the feeling of a very glamorous wedding. I was seated with Devon Lee Carlson, who was wearing a sheer Gucci number. Model Alex Consani came over to share some tea with us, and we attempted to make our way to the bar before being gently redirected. The speeches were about to begin, apparently, and the time for wandering was over.

The museum’s director introduced Eva Chow, who announced that this would be her final year helping to put on the gala. After years of bringing together the art and film communities, it was a rather poignant moment.

At a neighboring Gucci table sat François-Henri Pinault and his wife, Salma Hayek Pinault, in a sequin red gown by Gucci. Her waist was so dramatically cinched that she looked as though she had stepped straight out of an eighteenth-century portrait. Further along were Gucci creative director Demna, Kim Kardashian in a Bordeaux-hued sparkling gown, and Viola Davis, who was glowing. I also spotted 2hollis, who confessed that he didn’t know anyone there, so Devon and I immediately offered to adopt him for the evening.

There was also an impressive coterie of Victoria’s Secret Angels, including Elsa Hosk, Candice Swanepoel, and Rosie Huntington-Whiteley. Candice wore a Gucci gown held together by what appeared to be several strategically placed crystal strings in front of her crotch. Rosie had opted for a rather more revealing arrangement including a prominent display of her derrière with the Gucci logo doing some heavy lifting when it came to concealing her modesty. Later, I found several of the models outside smoking. Even angels need a cigarette.

In the bathroom, a woman in sky-high heels and a very tight Gucci gown was applying her lipstick. As she turned to leave, her clutch slipped from her hands and burst open on the floor. Its contents scattered in every direction, rolling underneath the neighboring stalls. Lipstick, a wallet, what I believe was a fake nail, and some medication. I admired her composure as she collected everything, composed her dignity, and returned to the party. The show must go on.

Back in the dining room, I said hello to my friend Noor Alfallah and Al Pacino. They were seated with Millicent Wilner, the senior director of Gagosian’s London gallery, who is one of my favorite people to run into every few months. On my way back to my seat, I passed Parker Posey, dressed in the most beautiful kaftan dripping in crystals, and I told her she looked gorgeous. By this point, I had begun mentally assembling my own fantasy dinner party featuring Jennifer Tilly, Parker Posey, and Kathy Hilton.

Eventually, the lights dimmed and the room fell quiet. A short film spotlighted Vija Celmins and her work. Based in New York, the artist spoke about her enduring fascination with the California coastline, the ocean, and the moon. She also mentioned that she had attended UCLA and, amusingly, had taken nothing from the experience. The room laughed at the accomplished artist delivering such an assessment, before she took the stage to accept the prestigious honor.

Next came Nicole Kidman, wearing a Chanel runway gown that immediately brought to mind Edgar Degas’s Little Dancer Aged Fourteen (1881). She spoke about Denis Villeneuve, admitting that while she has never actually appeared in any of his films, she’s an enormous admirer of his. “A few simple words and an image can stay with you long after the screen goes black,” she said.

We watched a montage of Villeneuve’s films, including Prisoners, Sicario, Blade Runner 2049, Arrival, Incendies and, of course, Dune. As someone who considers Sicario one of her all-time favorite films, I was particularly pleased to be there for this one.

When Villeneuve took the stage, he spoke about the importance of art in an age increasingly shaped by artificial intelligence. Images, he explained, had always spoken to him more profoundly than words. He recalled a visit to LACMA where the work of James Turrell served as inspiration for his film Arrival. Looking back, it is easy to see the connection: The enormous, mysterious spacecraft in the film has something of the quality of a Turrell light installation.

“Some artists use a paintbrush, I use a film crew,” he said.

It was a wonderful line, but his larger point was more affecting. He spoke about the importance of continuing to make art, particularly now, and about wanting to pass that belief on to his children.

Seated nearby were Timothée Chalamet and members of the casts of his films. I found myself looking around the room and thinking about the extraordinary concentration of talent gathered in one place. Vija Celmins, Denis Villeneuve, Al Pacino, Ed Ruscha: These are people who have spent their lives taking creative risks and changing the way we see things. There was something rather moving about sitting among them. For all the sequins, diamonds, and elaborate gowns, this was ultimately an evening celebrating people who had devoted themselves to making something that didn’t exist before.

After dinner, we were invited back outside for Rosé’s performance. Paris Hilton introduced her with an enthusiastic declaration of “That’s hot!” followed by “Sliving,” which felt like an appropriate transition from the intellectual rigors of the evening into the after-dark revelry. As we made our way outside, servers circulated with cotton candy, meringues, and miniature metal cups of caramel corn.

Devon and I made our way across Urban Light one last time, taking photographs beneath the lamps. She taught me how to use Burst mode on my phone, which was the most useful thing I learned all evening.

There were whispers of an after-party at Eva Chow’s house. I briefly considered going, then weighed the prospect against the fact that I was tired, had already spent several hours in a corseted state of social alertness, and was supposed to go home and write this very piece. Thankfully I have grown out of the kind of FOMO that comes with knowing a party is happening somewhere in Los Angeles without you. I headed home to crawl in bed with my cat.

On the drive back, I found myself thinking about Villeneuve’s speech. It is easy to get swept up in the spectacle of an evening like this. The clothes, the jewelry, the famous faces, the endless choreography of who is sitting with whom. But every so often, you’re reminded why these people are interesting in the first place.

After his speech, I will make it a point to see the final installment of Dune next month, and I can’t wait to see what he creates next. For now, I had a purple satin dress to hang up, photographs to look through, and a story to write. I fell asleep thinking about art, ambition, and all the things I might make if I were brave enough. All in due time.

François-Henri Pinault, Salma Hayek Pinault

Charles Porch, Aurora James, Robert Denning

Can't decide on a brew method? The Chefman Coffee Station Pro tackles them all. Yes, really.

In the age of the all-in-one appliance, maximizing countertop space just makes sense. In small kitchens especially, cramming half a dozen different-yet-similar appliances into limited space feels like such a waste. And sure, you don’t need both a blender and a food processor, but it’s nice to have the choice between the two. That’s why combo machines like the Ninja CrushBoss came out and started changing the game. That’s also the idea behind the Chefman Coffee Station Pro.

Unlike other x-in-one machines that incorporate a couple of different brewing methods (looking at you, Keurig K-Duo), the Chefman Coffee Station Pro combines 10 different functionalities into one machine. Craving a quick single cup? You can use it with both K-cups and Nespresso pods. Need to fill up a full carafe for a party? It does that, too. But what if you want to leisurely enjoy an iced latte or a shot of espresso on the weekend? Well, that’s also an option with the built-in manual espresso machine and automatic milk frother.

In terms of functionality, the Chefman Coffee Station Pro offers espresso, cappuccino, latte, single-serve coffee, 12-cup carafe, cold brew, cold-pressed espresso, coffee over ice, hot milk and cold foam. To try it out, I packed up all my other coffee makers and made it my primary coffee machine for two months.

You’d probably expect a machine with so many capabilities to be enormous, heavy, complicated, unwieldily. Not so with the Coffee Station Pro. It’s so simple to set up and use, I didn’t even need to read through the provided booklet before I was whipping up drinks. It also takes up barely more space than a dedicated espresso machine.

Right off the bat, I brewed a pot of drip coffee. First, I’m super impressed with the way the machine can read what I’m brewing based on the basket insert I choose. Pop in the drip basket, and it’s prompting me to choose the number of cups. Swap it out with the K-Cup pod holder, and it’s now asking how many ounces I’d like. It’s truly like magic!

Then, there’s the customization. First, pick between a single cup or a whole carafe. Then, choose to enjoy your coffee either hot or over ice. You also get the option of brewing a cup or a whole pot of cold brew for summertime get-togethers. There’s even a delay brew function, which makes it easy to prep your poison of choice the night before.

As I mentioned, the machine changes its touchscreen prompts based on which brew basket you choose. When you pop in a K-cup, you’re given the option of having it hot or over ice. There’s also a choice of 4-, 6-, 8-, 10- and 12-ounce cups. Then, you can adjust the strength and temperature, with three different settings for each. Finally, there’s a small flip-down platform to rest your cup on so that it doesn’t splash everywhere as it brews.

Want to use a Nespresso capsule instead? A pod insert pops into the K-cup adapter. Again, the machine will intuit this automatically and adjust accordingly. Overall, this aspect of the machine is incredibly intuitive. Plus, you can save specific settings as one of three “favorites,” if you want to speed things up with one-touch operation.

As for espressos, this thing does work. It boasts a 20-bar pressure system that brews espressos topped in a beautiful, silky crema. Pick from a single or double shot, or opt for a cappuccino or latte, both with a choice of single or double. If you choose a milk-based drink, ensure the milk reservoir is filled and angle the metal wand into your cup—the machine does the rest.

If you’re familiar with a standard manual espresso machine, you already know how to operate the portafilter. If not, no worries—there are helpful videos from Chefman to guide you through the process. You can also opt for hot milk, or warm or cold foam on its own by choosing the “froth” setting if you want to add any of those to your cup of regular coffee.

On the top of the machine next to the brew basket is an area with accessory storage for the portafilter baskets, Nespresso adapter and combination scoop/tamper. On the side of the coffee station is a place to stow the portafilter. While there’s no built-in storage for the brew basket, K-cup basket and carafe when they’re not in use, I do love that the smaller accessories have a dedicated space so they won’t be misplaced.

In terms of cleaning, this might be one of the easier machines I’ve ever used. All of the inserts simply rinse clean. But the part I really love is the milk frother. Instead of nooks and crannies that collect smells and residue, the entire thing comes apart into several pieces, so you can thoroughly rinse and wash every single part that touches milk. Win!

Chefman isn’t the only brand to claim that they’ve created an “all-in-one” solution for flexible baristas. In our research, we also found three other similar machines: The De’Longhi All-in-One, the Ninja Prestige Dual Brew Coffee Maker and, of course, the classic  Keurig K-Duo.

The only issue? We couldn’t find a single other appliance that offered K-Cup compatibility and Nespresso pod capability and a carafe and a manual espresso machine and automated milk frothing/latte settings. All of the options above offer at least two functions. Maybe four. But not all five. That crown belongs to the Chefman Coffee Station Pro alone.

Hopefully, we see more options pop up in the near future. But for now, the Chefman Coffee Station Pro is in its own category of coffee maker.

In my home, I used to have five different coffeemakers, including a Keurig, a Nespresso, an automatic espresso machine, a manual espresso maker and a classic drip coffeemaker. In fact, there were so many appliances that they began spilling into my dining room after I ran out of space on my dedicated coffee bar. After converting to the Chefman Coffee Station Pro, I’ve pared that number down to just one. One!

The only changes I’d make after using this machine since August 2026 are minor gripes. I do wish that there was a built-in coffee grinder, since having a separate bean grinder means having yet another appliance. And while I appreciate that there is a small storage cavity for tinier accessories, I don’t love having to find a place in my cupboard for the carafe and basket inserts when I’m not using them.

But honestly? Even with these small annoyances, I wouldn’t even knock off a full star on my final rating. The size, ease of use and cleanliness of the machine make it more than worth it—especially for flexible home baristas like me.

Condense five coffeemakers into just one with this ingenious appliance.

Want to clear up your counter space and join me in the future? You can snag this new appliance on the Chefman website or on Amazon. At $400, the Coffee Station Pro is absolutely an investment. And for some folks who won’t use all the different settings, it may not be worth the cost. But for coffee lovers who want to brew based on vibes (or who already have a long lineup of machines like I used to), the price point feels totally fair. After all, you’re getting five different machines in one!

The easier question is what can’t it make? It’s capable of espresso, single-serve coffee, a 12-cup carafe, cold brew and coffee over ice. While it’s not programmable to make specific drinks such as a cafe crema or Americano like some automatic espresso machines, the manual espresso component and automatic milk frother still offers extreme flexibility for budding baristas.

#6417. Slow-Cooker Tuscan Chicken

Creamy Tuscan chicken is a Delish classic—it’s by far one of our most-made meals. This slow-cooker variation is perfect for a busy fall night and has all of the flavors of the original—garlic, cherry tomatoes, oregano, and Parm—plus the added benefit of hands-off cooking. The other thing I love about this recipe (perhaps more than the original, but don't tell!) is that it uses bone-in chicken thighs, which are my favorite cut of chicken. Chicken breast is great for the OG stovetop version, but thighs are far more forgiving for low and slow heat, and they offer a little bit of extra flavor from the bone and skin.

The potatoes:When you have a creamy, delicious slow-cooker meal hot and ready to eat, the last thing you want to do is take out an extra pot to make a side dish, so we broke the Tuscan formula ever so slightly by adding baby potatoes to make this a well-rounded and hearty main and side all in one. It’s my new go-to on busy weeknights, and it provides all the comfort of the original, with even more oomph.

Storage:If you have any leftovers, store them in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 4 days.

#6416. BA’s Best Green Bean Casserole With Step-by-Step Video

This green bean casserole recipe skips the canned soup. Chris Morocco’s take on the classic Thanksgiving side pairs fresh green beans and deeply browned crimini mushrooms with a garlicky Parmesan béchamel. As for the topping, French’s fried onions are iconic for good reason, and they are staying right where they belong.

Give the mushrooms room to brown, salt the blanching water generously (like you would for cooking pasta), and taste the mushrooms and sauce before assembling. As written, you can cook the mushrooms and make the sauce at the same time. To save a pan, cook the mushrooms first, then transfer them to a plate and make the béchamel in the same pan, scraping up all the browned bits.

For the rest of the spread, turn to our classic Thanksgiving menu →

Can I make green bean casserole ahead of time?

Yes. Blanch the green beans, cook the mushrooms, and make the sauce up to 1 day ahead; cool and refrigerate them separately. Assemble and bake the day you plan to serve it, adding the fried onions during the final few minutes of baking.

We don’t recommend freezing the assembled casserole—the cream sauce can separate, and the beans turn mushy after thawing and reheating.

How do I keep the cream sauce from separating?

Don’t overreduce it. Once the béchamel is thick and bubbling, take it off the heat before whisking in the garlic and Parmesan. Boiling off too much liquid can cause the fat to separate. Stick with the recipe’s amount of Parmesan, too—extra cheese can contribute to a broken sauce.

Blanched, fresh beans are our first choice, but readers have reported success with frozen petite and French-cut beans. We haven’t tested the swap, but recommend thawing them overnight in your refrigerator and straining the excess liquid before continuing.

Can I make this green bean casserole gluten-free?

We haven’t tested a gluten-free version, but our editors suggest replacing the all-purpose flour with a gluten-free flour blend. You’ll also need to seek out gluten-free fried onions, or try our flourless Crispy Fried Shallots.

Place rack in middle of oven; preheat oven to 375°. Working in batches, cook 2 lb. fresh green beans in a large pot of boiling salted water until bright green and halfway to tenderness, about 3 minutes per batch. Drain and let cool; trim stem ends.

Heat 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Cook ½ lb. crimini mushrooms, sliced, without stirring, until golden brown underneath, about 2 minutes. Toss and continue to cook, tossing occasionally, until browned on both sides, about 3 minutes more. Add 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter and 2 large thyme sprigs to pan. Cook, tossing occasionally, until butter browns and mushrooms are dark brown and very tender, about 4 minutes longer. Season with kosher salt and transfer to a plate. Repeat with 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter, salt, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, ½ lb. crimini mushrooms, sliced, and 2 large thyme sprigs.

Melt remaining 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large saucepan over medium-low. Whisk in 2 Tbsp. all-purpose flour and cook, whisking occasionally, until roux is golden brown and smells mildly nutty, about 4 minutes. Whisk in 1¼ cups whole milk and 1 cup heavy cream. Increase heat and bring to a simmer, whisking often, and cook until béchamel sauce is thick and bubbling, about 5 minutes. Remove from heat and whisk in 4 garlic cloves, finely grated, and ½ cup grated Parmesan; season with salt and freshly ground pepper.

Arrange green beans and mushrooms in a 2-qt. baking dish. Pour sauce over bean mixture (it may not look like enough, but it will get saucier as it bakes). Cover tightly with foil and bake until sauce is bubbling, 25–30 minutes. Uncover and continue to bake until casserole is lightly browned on top and around the edges, 15–20 minutes longer. Top with ¾ cup French’s fried onions and continue to bake just until onions are slightly darker and fragrant, about 3 minutes. Let sit 10 minutes to set before serving.

#6415. From the Archives: When Iowa Governor-Elect Rob Sand Was Shot by Steven Meisel for Vogue Italia

“Be My Baby,” by Steven Meisel, was originally published in the February 2004 issue of Vogue Italia.

For more of the best from Vogue’s archive, sign up for our Nostalgia newsletter here.

With a fluffed-up quiff and a supermodel on his arm, here’s a look at Iowa’s next governor. Long before Democrat Rob Sand made political history, he was having a very different kind of moment in the spotlight, posing for Steven Meisel in the pages of Vogue Italia.

The year was 2004, and Sand was among the fresh faces who appeared in “Be My Baby,” an editorial in the February issue, photographed by Meisel and styled by Brana Wolf. Alongside Sand was a cast of rising fashion stars, including a young Caroline Trentini, with whom he posed in a series of moody, black-and-white portraits.

The concept centered on a romanticized vision of 1950s youth culture, abounding with the aforementioned rockabilly hair and lots of leather The original Italian introduction described the mood as a collision of bon ton—good manners and traditional propriety—and transgression.

Garren was responsible for the towering and teased hairstyles, while Dame Pat McGrath crafted smudgy, kohl-rimmed eyes. The cast wore Belstaff leather biker jackets, white Guess T-shirts and jeans, Helmut Lang tank tops and tailoring, Prada separates, and a Gucci crocodile belt. Womenswear included diaphanous Blumarine slips, Prada silk and tweed, and chiffon dresses by Rossella Tarabini for Anna Molinari.

“Was a fun day!” Sand wrote beneath an Instagram post by Meisel revisiting the shoot.

Sand’s modeling career was no mere college dalliance. While studying political science at Brown University, the six-foot-three Iowan spent time working in Milan and Paris, walking for Prada, cult Japanese label Number (N)ine, and Giuliano Fujiwara. He also appeared in Prada’s spring 2003 menswear show. In fact, his fashion commitments were once so serious that he missed the 2004 Iowa caucuses in his hometown of Decorah because he was working in Milan.

On November 3, Sand defeated Republican Zach Lahn to become the first Democrat elected governor of Iowa in 20 years, following two terms as state auditor. His newly resurfaced modeling portfolio has since become an unlikely internet sensation. Sand himself has joined in on the joke, sharing one of his old Vogue Italia photographs with the caption: “I’m disappointed to learn images of me modeling for Prada are circulating. Because this shot from Italian Vogue is much better.”

From Prada to public office, it’s quite the career trajectory. And with his campaign now selling “My Model Governor” merchandise, Rob Sand clearly knows how to harness a good fashion moment.

If you’re shopping for a true foodie, nothing can top a gourmet gift basket. But if you go that route, you have to do your research. After all, not all food gifts are the same. Instead, for something ready-to-eat, opt for beloved foods with an established fanbase—perhaps one of the editor-loved finds on Goldbelly. Or, if you want to really impress them, high-quality ingredients are sure to inspire their culinary creativity. That’s why my go-to food gift is an olive oil gift set from Enzo’s Table.

The Signature Selection gift set offers a diverse lineup of flavors to impress your favorite foodies.

Folks at Enzo’s Table have been farming their vineyard in California’s fertile San Joaquin Valley for nearly a century. This gives their gourmand products a farm-to-table feel that’s backed by decades of know-how. In fact, over the years, the brand has proudly received over 200 awards for its signature olive oils, jams and biscotti!

The Signature Selection olive oil gift set is a fleet consisting of four of Enzo’s famous olive oils, plus their signature balsamic vinegar. All five 100ml bottles are organic, having been produced in the San Joaquin Valley vineyard. The gift set contains the following:

The Delicate EVOO offers a buttery flavor and incredibly mild yet peppery finish, making it a perfectly smooth pick for dipping bread or incorporating into salad dressings. Enzo’s Basil Crush EVOO is, as you’d expect, herby and earthy. It’s another option that’s particularly good for roasts, especially red meats. I also love adding a splash on caprese salad.

The Traditional Balsamic Vinegar is incredibly versatile in all the ways you love to see with balsamic. Because it’s crafted from sweet, organic Lambrusco and Trebbiano grapes, it shines brightest on summery dishes like grilled fruits and balsamic Brussels sprouts. I’ve tried a lot of balsamic over the years, and this one might be the thickest, richest blend I’ve enjoyed.

Delight your favorite foodie with a full fleet of flavors when you gift them an Enzo Olive Oil gift set!

#6411. Chili Crisp Yogurt Chicken

Slather Greek yogurt and your favorite chili crisp on chicken thighs, roast in a hot oven, and you’ll be rewarded with juicy, tender meat with a delightful orange-tinged exterior. But the best part of this sheet-pan dinner comes after the chicken is cooked: Spread cooked rice into the pan’s juices, then slide the baking sheet back into the oven. As the rice soaks up the deeply savory sauce, it will crisp in spots, creating a texture that’s somewhere between chewy-fluffy steamed grains and a freshly toasted pita chip. And when it comes to chili crisp, we love the iconic and easy-to-source Lao Gan Ma, but specialty brands like Fly By Jing are great too—just make sure the one you use is not too spicy, which will overpower the dish.

More great chicken and rice recipes this way: One-Pot Chicken Thighs With Cilantro Rice and Beans; Spiced Coconut Chicken Rice; Nana’s Chicken and Rice Stew.

Preheat oven to 425°. Season 6–8 skinless, boneless chicken thighs (1½–2 lb.) with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt.

Whisk together ¾ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt and ¼ cup plus 2 Tbsp. well-stirred chili crisp in a large bowl. Add chicken thighs and toss to coat.

Arrange chicken on a rimmed baking sheet and top with any yogurt mixture left in bowl. Bake chicken until deeply browned and an instant-read thermometer inserted into the thickest part of a thigh registers 165°, 25–30 minutes. Transfer chicken to a cutting board or plate.

Spread 3 cups cooked jasmine or short-grain rice over baking sheet with chicken juices and bake until most of the juices have been absorbed and rice is starting to crisp in spots, 12–15 minutes.

Meanwhile, whisk together 1 Tbsp. finely grated lime zest, ¼ cup fresh lime juice, ½ tsp. sugar, ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt, and remaining ¼ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt in a small bowl.

Combine ½ medium head of green cabbage (about 1 lb.), very thinly sliced, and a big pinch of Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt in a large bowl. Using your hands, scrunch cabbage gently to soften. Add 1 small red onion, thinly sliced, 1 cup finely chopped cilantro, and yogurt dressing and toss to combine. Taste cabbage slaw and season with more salt if needed.

Slice chicken as desired and serve with crisped rice and cabbage slaw.

#6410. For Talarico and Hinojosa, Whataburger Is a Perfectly Texas Place to Celebrate

Like so many Texans on so many nights, Senator-elect James Talarico and Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa ended their evening at Whataburger.

Late Tuesday night, after Talarico flipped a Senate seat for the Democrats and Hinojosa was elected the first Democratic governor of the state in more than three decades, the two sat down at an Austin-area location of Whataburger, the iconic regional fast food chain, to clink plastic orange-and-white-striped cups.

It was a fitting setting for the pair, who played critical roles in the blue wave that swept the country in the midterm elections on Tuesday night. Talarico, who defeated scandal-plagued Republican Ken Paxton, went on the offensive against billionaires, prevailing with a positive, populist message against a party funded by Elon Musk and other ultrawealthy donors.

Hinojosa, the first Latina to be elected governor for Texas, targeted corruption and data centers in her race against Republican incumbent Greg Abbott. Both Talarico and Hinojosa will be the first Democrats in more than 30 years to serve Texas in their respective roles.

But even in the midst of a polarizing political moment for the nation, loving Whataburger is bigger than politics in Texas. Since opening its first location in Corpus Christi, Texas, in 1950, the chain, with its signature A-frame buildings, has become a social center for small towns, a place for a budget-friendly meal for families, and a crucial hangout for high schoolers figuring out where else they’ll go that night or stopping for a late-night breakfast before heading home.

Instead of popping Champagne, it’s poignant that Talarico and Hinojosa celebrated with oversize sodas. You can still get a double-burger Whatameal for under $15. These aren't the first Democrats to harness the tangy-sweet appeal of Whataburger's much-beloved Fancy Ketchup. In 2018, the campaign for senate-hopeful Beto O'Rourke shared video of him skateboarding outside a Whataburger before going inside to eat.

Today’s prices are squarely in line with the affordability politics that resonated with voters this cycle. And Talarico and Hinojosa’s Whataburger cheers was a fitting end to a campaign that wove food and politics together. While casting himself as a David against Paxton’s Goliath, Talarico absorbed attacks that claimed he was vegan. While the Senator-elect had urged residents to cut down on beef consumption, he denied the dietary restriction, countering by posting pictures of himself chowing down on barbecue.

Paxton still tried to label his opponent as “Tofu Talarico,” and Trump imagined a scenario where Talarico excuses himself to vomit after eating meat. The barbs were not-so-subtle assaults on Talarico’s manhood, the latest manifestation of the link between meat and masculinity. But there was Talarico on election night, sitting in the house of beef patties, Whatachick’n strips, and bacon-and-egg taquitos.

After a 2019 acquisition by a Chicago-based investment firm, Whataburger has faced allegations of diminishing quality and a nascent rival in Austin’s P. Terry’s Burger Stand. And still, aside from a Dairy Queen or A&W after a high school football game, there may be nowhere in Texas that feels as Texas as a Whataburger when you’re not quite ready to call it a night.

One of the defining features of Whataburger has always been its friendliness to customizing your meal—made to order. Want jalapeños and mustard on your burger, no mayo? Go right ahead, sweetie.

On Tuesday night, as part of national rebuke to President Donald Trump’s party, Texas made its choice clear.
